set_title: CLAT PG Practice Set 04 (New Criminal Laws: BNS, BNSS, BSA with Constitution, Theories and Related Laws; Trap-Annotated)

pattern.ordering: New criminal laws (BNS, BNSS, BSA) read with constitutional provisions, theories and authors of jurisprudence and criminology, and related special laws
pattern.note: Practice set, not a mock; original passages and questions (none taken from Mock 01-06, Practice Sets 01-03). The official paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes; this set is longer for extra practice.

subjects_covered: Criminal Law, Privacy and Free Speech
Law of Evidence and Constitutional Law
Special Criminal Laws and Constitutional Law
instructions: Each question has four options and exactly one correct answer.
Correct answer carries 1 mark; each wrong answer carries -0.25.

Passages are original summaries for practice, current to mid-November 2026. Verify pending or evolving matters (e.g. BNS s.106(2) hit-and-run status, the BNS s.152 challenge, the marital-rape challenge, review proceedings on the PMLA ruling, scope of BNSS s.479 for old cases) against current official sources.
Every explanation includes why the other options fail, the CLAT trap, and any language trick.

passages.title: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: Commencement, Savings and Article 20(1)
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and came into force on 1 July 2024. Offences committed before that date continue to be tried under the Penal Code, because Article 20(1) forbids conviction for an act that was not an offence when done and forbids a penalty greater than the one in force at that time. The Court has accepted that an accused may take the benefit of a later ameliorative provision, as in T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe (1983). The Sanhita introduces community service as a form of punishment, creates the offences of organised crime, petty organised crime and terrorist act, and punishes murder by a group of five or more persons on specified grounds. It does not retain adultery, which the Supreme Court struck down in Joseph Shine (2018) under Articles 14, 15 and 21, nor the old provision on unnatural offences, which Navtej Singh Johar (2018) had earlier read down for consenting adults. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs had recommended in November 2023 that a gender-neutral adultery offence and a provision on non-consensual unnatural acts be retained, but Parliament did not accept that recommendation. Because criminal law and criminal procedure are in the Concurrent List (Entries 1 and 2), a State may amend the Sanhita for its own territory, subject to Article 254 and the assent of the President where it is repugnant to the Union law. A Standing Committee's report is a recommendation; its non-acceptance does not by itself affect the validity of the Act.

questions.question: A man commits an offence in March 2024 for which the Sanhita prescribes a heavier penalty than the Penal Code. He is tried in 2025. On the passage, the highest penalty he can receive is

options.A: the one prescribed by the Penal Code, because Article 20(1) bars a penalty greater than the one in force when the act was done
options.B: the Penal Code penalty, but only if the Standing Committee had recommended it
options.C: the heavier penalty of the Sanhita, because the trial took place after 1 July 2024
options.D: the heavier penalty of the Sanhita, since sentencing is a matter of procedure and not of substance

questions.explanation: The second limb of Article 20(1) fixes the ceiling by the date of the act. The date of trial is irrelevant.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C uses the date of trial. Option D treats sentence as procedure, which the passage rejects. Option B makes a legislative committee's view a condition, which has no constitutional basis.
questions.clat_trap: Students see that the trial happens under the new Code and assume the new penalty applies. The constitutional test looks to the date of the act.
questions.language_trick: 'for which ... heavier penalty' signals the second limb of Article 20(1).

questions.question: A State legislature wishes to amend the Sanhita to enhance the penalty for an offence within its territory. On the passage, such a law

options.A: is within competence only if Parliament first repeals the corresponding provision
options.B: is outside competence because criminal law is exclusively a Union subject in List I
options.C: is within competence and prevails automatically over the Union law in the State, so that no assent of the President is needed even where it is repugnant
options.D: is within competence as criminal law is in the Concurrent List, but is subject to Article 254 and Presidential assent if repugnant to the Union law

questions.explanation: Entries 1 and 2 of List III allow State amendments. Repugnancy is resolved under Article 254, and a State law prevails only with Presidential assent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats criminal law as a Union subject. Option C ignores the assent requirement under Article 254(2). Option A invents a repeal precondition.
questions.clat_trap: The words 'Concurrent List' are known but the assent mechanism is forgotten, so the option which says 'prevails automatically' attracts.
questions.language_trick: 'repugnant' triggers Article 254, not a general bar.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement on the passage?

options.A: Parliament accepted the Standing Committee's recommendation for a gender-neutral adultery offence, so the Sanhita retains it
options.B: Joseph Shine struck down adultery under Articles 14, 15 and 21
options.C: Offences committed before 1 July 2024 continue to be tried and punished under the Penal Code, subject to the Article 20(1) benefit
options.D: Community service is recognised as a form of punishment in the Sanhita

questions.explanation: The passage says Parliament did not accept the recommendation and that the Sanhita does not retain adultery. The first option is therefore the false statement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option B and Option C each restate the passage correctly.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem makes the false statement the answer. The false option is the only one that is plausible-sounding because Committee reports are often assumed to be followed.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT a correct statement' reverses the usual search.

questions.question: The Standing Committee's report on the Sanhita is best described as

options.A: a condition of the President's assent which must be fulfilled before the Act is valid
options.B: a binding direction whose rejection invalidates the Act under Article 13
options.C: a recommendation that Parliament was free to reject
options.D: a judicial finding that binds courts under Article 141 of the Constitution

questions.explanation: The report is advisory. Parliament may accept or reject it, and rejection does not affect validity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats an advisory report as law. Option D confuses a parliamentary committee with a court. Option A invents a condition for assent.
questions.clat_trap: Committee reports are described in a heavy vocabulary, which tempts the student to treat them as binding.
questions.language_trick: The passage ends with 'a recommendation'; the answer simply repeats it.

questions.question: Navtej Singh Johar and Joseph Shine are relevant to the drafting of the Sanhita because

options.A: both decisions had already narrowed or removed provisions of the earlier Code, on the footing of Articles 14, 15 and 21, which the Sanhita did not carry forward
options.B: both directed Parliament to omit the provisions from any new Code within a year
options.C: both held that Parliament may never legislate on sexual conduct between adults
options.D: both were decided under Article 20(1) and concerned retrospective penalty

questions.explanation: Navtej read down the old unnatural offences provision and Joseph Shine struck down adultery, so the Sanhita did not reproduce them in their earlier form.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C is an overstatement. Option B invents a direction to Parliament. Option D misidentifies the Articles involved.
questions.clat_trap: 'Narrowed or removed' mixes two different outcomes, which a hurried reader takes as imprecision.
questions.language_trick: 'earlier form' is the hedge in the right option.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A person who committed an offence in 2023 cannot be punished with a penalty found only in the Sanhita. Reason (R): Article 20(1) prohibits a penalty greater than the one in force at the time of the offence.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A follows from R. The ceiling is fixed by the law at the time of the act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a true constitutional rule and supplies the reason for A.
questions.clat_trap: Because the Sanhita is new, students look for a reason on commencement, not on Article 20(1).
questions.language_trick: 'only in the Sanhita' narrows the assertion to a penalty that did not exist earlier.

passages.title: Why Punish? Theories of Punishment and the Sanhita
passages.passage: Theories of punishment answer the question why the State may inflict suffering on an offender. Retributive theories, associated with Kant and Hegel, justify punishment by desert: Kant insisted that a person may never be punished merely as a means to a social end, while Hegel saw punishment as the annulment of the wrong. Deterrent theories, developed by Beccaria in On Crimes and Punishments (1764) and by Bentham, justify punishment by its effect on future conduct; Beccaria stressed the certainty and promptness of punishment over its severity, and Bentham treated punishment as an evil justified only if it prevents a greater one. Reformative theories aim at rehabilitation; in Mohd. Giasuddin v. State of A.P. (1977), Krishna Iyer J. said that the sentencing approach should be to humanise and reform. H.L.A. Hart, in Punishment and Responsibility, separated the general justifying aim of punishment from the principles governing its distribution, such as the requirement of responsibility. In Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983), a Bench of five judges struck down the mandatory death sentence for murder by a life convict, holding that a sentence fixed without any opportunity to consider circumstances violates Articles 14 and 21. Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which deals with murder by a life convict, prescribes death or imprisonment for life, leaving the choice to the court. Bachan Singh (1980) confines the death penalty to the rarest of rare cases, and the Sanhita's new punishment of community service is often described as consistent with the reformative approach. Articles 72 and 161 preserve the executive power of mercy.

questions.question: A legislature prescribes a very severe punishment for an offence but few offenders are ever caught or tried promptly. A follower of Beccaria would criticise this because

options.A: he treated desert as the only justification, so prevention plays no part
options.B: he required the offender to be fully reformed before any punishment could be imposed on him
options.C: he regarded all punishment as an annulment of the wrong done, so severity and prevention are irrelevant to it
options.D: he valued the certainty and promptness of punishment above its severity as a means of prevention

questions.explanation: Beccaria is a deterrence theorist who stressed certainty and promptness over severity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C is Hegel's view. Option A is the retributive stance of Kant. Option B is a reformative idea attributed to no one in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Names and schools are swapped across options, so the student must attach the right idea to Beccaria.
questions.language_trick: 'above its severity' states a comparison, not a rejection of severity altogether.

questions.question: A judge sentences an offender solely because the offender 'deserves' it, ignoring effect on others and on the offender's future. This is most consistent with

options.A: the retributive theory associated with Kant, which justifies punishment by desert and not by its social consequences
options.B: the deterrent theory of Bentham, which justifies punishment only by the harm it prevents
options.C: the general justifying aim in Hart's work, which looks to the benefits of the system
options.D: the reformative approach in Giasuddin, which aims at the rehabilitation of the offender

questions.explanation: Desert-based sentencing, indifferent to consequences, is retributive.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B looks to consequences. Option D looks to rehabilitation. Option C is a utilitarian justifying aim.
questions.clat_trap: All four options are theories of punishment, so the student must separate desert from consequence.
questions.language_trick: 'solely because ... deserves' pinpoints desert.

questions.question: Mithu v State of Punjab is relevant to section 104 of the Sanhita because

options.A: Mithu held that the death penalty is unconstitutional in every case of murder, whoever the offender may be and whatever the facts
options.B: the Sanhita leaves the court a choice between death and imprisonment for life, avoiding the defect of a mandatory sentence
options.C: Mithu directed Parliament to abolish all special punishment for life convicts
options.D: Mithu upheld a mandatory death sentence for life convicts as a valid deterrent measure serving the interest of society and public order

questions.explanation: Mithu struck down the mandatory sentence, and section 104 leaves discretion between two sentences.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the holding. Option A overstates it. Option C invents a direction to Parliament.
questions.clat_trap: A reversal of the holding is the classic trap; the student must recall that the mandatory feature was struck down, not the sentence itself.
questions.language_trick: 'mandatory' is the key word.

questions.question: On Hart's distinction, the principle that only a responsible person may be punished belongs to

options.A: neither question, because Hart rejected responsibility as a condition of punishment
options.B: the general justifying aim, since responsibility is the purpose for which punishment exists
options.C: the distribution of punishment, not its general justifying aim
options.D: the general justifying aim, which Hart defined in terms of reformation of the offender

questions.explanation: Hart placed responsibility among the principles of distribution, while the general justifying aim is about the benefits of the practice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D misdefines the general aim. Option B merges the two questions. Option A attributes to Hart the opposite of his view.
questions.clat_trap: Hart's two-part structure is often collapsed in memory into one question.
questions.language_trick: 'distribution' versus 'justifying aim' is the central contrast.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: Mohd. Giasuddin supports an approach to sentencing which aims to humanise and reform
options.B: Bachan Singh makes the death penalty the usual sentence for murder, with imprisonment for life as an exception which needs special reasons
options.C: Articles 72 and 161 preserve the executive power of mercy
options.D: Bentham treated punishment as an evil justified only if it prevents a greater evil

questions.explanation: The passage says Bachan Singh confines the death penalty to the rarest of rare cases, which makes life the rule.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option A and Option C are all consistent with the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem, with the false option phrased in the vocabulary of 'special reasons' (which appears in the real statute), invites acceptance.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT consistent' reverses the task.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the passage. I. Kant allowed punishment of a person purely as a means of deterring others. II. Beccaria preferred the certainty of punishment to its severity. III. Mithu held that a mandatory death sentence for a life convict violates Articles 14 and 21. IV. Section 104 of the Sanhita makes death the only sentence for murder by a life convict. Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and IV only
options.B: II only
options.C: II and III only
options.D: I, II and III only

questions.explanation: II and III restate the passage. I contradicts Kant's position and IV contradicts the discretion in section 104.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: I reverses Kant. IV says death is the only sentence, which the passage contradicts. Options which include either are wrong.
questions.clat_trap: A four-statement combination rewards partial knowledge, and the option 'II only' tempts those who are unsure of III.
questions.language_trick: 'only' in IV makes the statement false.

passages.title: Mens Rea, Incapacity and General Exceptions in the Sanhita
passages.passage: A crime ordinarily requires a guilty act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea). The Supreme Court held in State of Maharashtra v. M.H. George (1965) that mens rea may be excluded by a statute, expressly or by necessary implication, particularly in offences meant to protect public welfare, such as the foreign exchange control provisions in issue there. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita grounds exculpation on incapacity and mistake. A child below seven years is immune absolutely (section 20); a child between seven and twelve is immune if the child has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of the conduct (section 21); and a person of unsound mind is protected under section 22 if, at the time of the act, he was incapable of knowing its nature or that it was wrong or contrary to law. In Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakker v. State of Gujarat (1964), the Court held that the burden of proving legal insanity is on the accused, who may discharge it by showing a preponderance of probability, and that medical insanity is different from legal insanity. Intoxication is a defence under section 23 only where the intoxicant was administered without the person's knowledge or against his will. A mistake of fact made in good faith, believing oneself bound by law, is excused under section 14, while a mistake about the law is not. H.L.A. Hart linked these exceptions to the idea that punishment should be reserved for those who had a fair opportunity to choose lawful conduct.

questions.question: A, aged ten, takes a neighbour's bicycle and sells it, fully understanding that the act is wrong. On the passage, A

options.A: is not protected by the immunity for children aged seven to twelve, since he had sufficient maturity of understanding
options.B: is wholly immune under the provision that applies to a child below seven years, because he was a child when he did the act at all in law
options.C: is protected, since the immunity depends on age alone and not on understanding
options.D: is wholly immune, because a child below twelve cannot commit any offence under the Sanhita, whatever his understanding of the act

questions.explanation: Section 21 protects a child of seven to twelve only if the child lacks sufficient maturity of understanding. A understood the nature and consequence of his act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D treats age as absolute immunity up to twelve. Option B applies the wrong age band. Option C ignores the maturity test.
questions.clat_trap: The age band attracts a blanket-immunity answer; the maturity condition in the middle band is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'sufficient maturity of understanding' is the statutory condition.

questions.question: C is given a drink laced without his knowledge by a rival and, while incapable of knowing the nature of his act, commits what would ordinarily be an offence. On the passage, C

options.A: is liable, because intoxication, whether voluntary or not, is never a defence
options.B: is protected only if he proves medical insanity beyond reasonable doubt
options.C: may be protected, because intoxication administered without his knowledge or against his will is a defence under section 23 where it deprives him of that knowledge
options.D: is liable, since a mistake about the law is not excused

questions.explanation: Involuntary intoxication, which removes knowledge of the nature of the act, is the case the section protects.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the rule for voluntary intoxication as if it covered all. Option B confuses intoxication with insanity and misstates the standard. Option D brings in a different principle.
questions.clat_trap: Voluntary and involuntary intoxication are lumped together in memory, which makes the first option attractive.
questions.language_trick: 'without his knowledge or against his will' is the statutory phrase.

questions.question: In Dahyabhai Thakker, the burden of proving legal insanity

options.A: lies on the accused, who must prove it beyond reasonable doubt like any element of the offence
options.B: lies on the accused, on a preponderance of probability
options.C: does not arise, since medical insanity alone is a complete defence under the Sanhita
options.D: lies on the prosecution, which must negative insanity beyond reasonable doubt in every case

questions.explanation: The Court placed the burden on the accused and set the standard at preponderance of probability.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D places the burden on the prosecution. Option A raises the standard. Option C confuses medical insanity with legal insanity.
questions.clat_trap: Burden and standard are two separate questions; options mix them.
questions.language_trick: 'preponderance of probability' is the standard.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct statement of M.H. George as described in the passage?

options.A: Mens rea is excluded only where the statute expressly says so in so many words
options.B: Mens rea is relevant only in offences which carry a sentence of imprisonment
options.C: Mens rea is an essential element of every offence in every situation, whatever the statute says
options.D: Mens rea can be excluded by a statute by necessary implication

questions.explanation: The Court accepted exclusion by express words or by necessary implication, particularly in public welfare offences.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C makes mens rea absolute. Option A limits exclusion to express words. Option B ties it to the type of sentence.
questions.clat_trap: 'Express' versus 'by necessary implication' is a one-phrase difference.
questions.language_trick: 'by necessary implication' is the decisive phrase.

questions.question: E, a foreigner, assumes that an act is lawful in India because it is lawful in his own country and does it. On the passage, E

options.A: is not excused, since a mistake about the law is no defence, unlike a good-faith mistake of fact
options.B: is excused, because a good-faith mistake of any kind, whether of fact or of law, removes the mens rea of the offence
options.C: is excused only if he is below the age of twelve years
options.D: is excused, provided he proves the belief by a preponderance of probability, as an accused pleading insanity must do in his case

questions.explanation: Section 14 deals with mistake of fact. A mistake about the law is not excused.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B extends the defence to all mistakes. Option D borrows the standard for insanity. Option C brings in an irrelevant age condition.
questions.clat_trap: Mistake of fact and mistake of law share a word; the student must separate them.
questions.language_trick: 'good faith' is attached only to mistake of fact.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A mistake of law made in good faith is a complete defence under the Sanhita. Reason (R): Section 14 excuses an act done by a person who, by reason of a mistake of fact, believes himself bound by law to do it.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because the passage says a mistake about the law is not excused. R states section 14 correctly.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A fails on the passage. R is true but does not support A.
questions.clat_trap: R is a true statement placed beside a false assertion, so a hasty reader chooses the first or second option.
questions.language_trick: 'of law' in A versus 'of fact' in R is the whole difference.

passages.title: Murder, Mob Lynching and Negligent Death under the Sanhita
passages.passage: Murder (section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) is a species of culpable homicide (section 105): the act must be done with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing bodily injury which the offender knows is likely to cause death, or injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death. Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958) explains the third limb: once an injury is intentional and objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the offender's lack of intention to cause death is irrelevant. Culpable homicide is not murder where an exception applies, such as grave and sudden provocation or exceeding the right of private defence in good faith. Section 103(1) punishes murder with death or imprisonment for life and fine. Section 103(2) addresses murder by a group of five or more persons acting together on the ground of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief, and carries death or imprisonment for life with fine; it followed directions in Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India (2018), where the Court listed preventive, remedial and punitive measures against mob lynching and invited Parliament to create a specific offence. Section 106(1) punishes causing death by negligence; Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) required gross negligence before a doctor could be held criminally liable. Section 106(2), on a driver who flees without reporting, is reported to have been held in abeyance in 2024 (verify current status). Section 108 punishes abetment of suicide.

questions.question: A strikes B on the leg with a heavy rod, intending only to cause a serious injury. The injury is, in the ordinary course of nature, sufficient to cause death, and B dies. A did not intend death. On the passage, A

options.A: is guilty of causing death by negligence under section 106(1) and nothing more, because no intention to kill was ever present
options.B: is not guilty of any homicide offence since the leg is not a vital part
options.C: may be guilty of murder, since the intended injury was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature
options.D: is guilty only of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, since he did not intend to cause death but only to cause a serious injury

questions.explanation: Virsa Singh holds that the offender's lack of intention to cause death is irrelevant where an intended injury is objectively sufficient to cause death.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D requires intention to kill, which the third limb does not. Option A treats an intended injury as mere negligence. Option B is an anatomical argument that the test does not use.
questions.clat_trap: The student's instinct is that intention to kill decides murder; the third limb requires only intention to cause the injury.
questions.language_trick: 'intending only' in the stem invites the mistaken answer.

questions.question: Which of the following situations falls within section 103(2)?

options.A: Three persons act together and kill a man on the ground of his religion
options.B: Six persons act together and beat a man to death on the ground of his caste, in a case that falls within the group-murder provision for five or more persons
options.C: Six persons act together and kill a man in order to rob him of his wallet
options.D: Five persons kill a man over a boundary dispute with a neighbour

questions.explanation: Section 103(2) needs five or more persons acting together and a specified ground. Only the first fact pattern supplies both.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A has fewer than five persons. Option C has no specified ground. Option D also lacks a specified ground.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option has one element but not both, so the student must check number and ground together.
questions.language_trick: 'five or more' and 'ground' are conjunctive.

questions.question: Tehseen Poonawalla bears on section 103(2) because

options.A: the Court suggested measures and urged Parliament to create a specific offence, as the Sanhita later did
options.B: the Court struck down the earlier law on mob violence as violating Article 21 and left a gap for Parliament to fill
options.C: the Court itself created the offence of mob lynching under Article 142 and Parliament merely reproduced it in the Sanhita
options.D: the Court held that Parliament has no power to legislate on mob violence

questions.explanation: The Court invited Parliament to legislate. The Sanhita's group-murder provision followed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C credits the Court with legislating. Option B invents an earlier law that was struck down. Option D denies legislative power.
questions.clat_trap: The Court's directions and the legislative response are two steps; the options skip or reverse one.
questions.language_trick: 'invited' versus 'created' is the key distinction.

questions.question: A doctor operates with ordinary skill but a rare complication causes the patient's death. On the passage, criminal liability under section 106(1) is

options.A: likely, because section 106(1) applies in the same manner to all procedures
options.B: certain, because the Sanhita denies doctors the defence of consent
options.C: unlikely, because Jacob Mathew requires gross negligence, and not mere error of judgment or an unfortunate result of treatment, before a doctor is criminally liable
options.D: likely, because any death in the course of treatment amounts to negligence

questions.explanation: Jacob Mathew requires gross negligence for a doctor's criminal liability. A rare complication despite ordinary skill is not gross negligence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D equates a bad outcome with negligence. Option A ignores the special standard for doctors. Option B invents a bar on consent.
questions.clat_trap: Outcome-bias leads the student to hold the doctor liable because a patient died.
questions.language_trick: 'gross' is the qualifier that matters.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct on the passage?

options.A: Section 106(2) is in force in all respects, and its status needs no further verification
options.B: Section 108 punishes abetment of suicide
options.C: Section 103(1) prescribes death or imprisonment for life, and fine, for the offence of murder under section 101
options.D: Culpable homicide is not murder where grave and sudden provocation applies

questions.explanation: The passage says section 106(2) is reported to have been held in abeyance and asks the reader to verify its status.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C, Option D and Option B are correct on the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A recent-events caveat is easy to miss, and the false option sounds like a routine statement of law.
questions.language_trick: 'in all respects' is an absolute that the passage does not support.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. I. Murder is a species of culpable homicide. II. Under section 103(2), a group of two or more persons suffices. III. Under Virsa Singh, lack of intention to cause death is irrelevant where an intended injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. IV. Jacob Mathew requires only simple negligence for the criminal liability of doctors. Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: III and IV only

questions.explanation: I and III restate the passage. II understates the numerical threshold and IV understates the standard.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II says two or more persons, against five or more. IV says simple negligence, against gross negligence.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong statement is a one-word alteration of a correct one (two for five; simple for gross).
questions.language_trick: 'two or more' and 'simple' are the altered words.

passages.title: Children and Sexual Offences: POCSO, the Sanhita and Articles 15(3), 21
passages.passage: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 defines a child as a person below eighteen years and creates gender-neutral offences of penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault and sexual harassment. It places a duty on any person who knows of an offence to report it, presumes in section 29 that the accused committed the offence once the foundational facts are shown, and under section 42A overrides inconsistent laws. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, a woman's consent is immaterial if she is below eighteen, and the exception to the offence of rape protects only intercourse with a wife who is eighteen or more, an alignment which followed Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017). In Attorney General v. Satish (2021) the Supreme Court held that the offence of sexual assault requires sexual intent, and not skin-to-skin contact, so that touching a child's body through clothing can attract the offence. In Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish (2024), the Court held that storing or viewing child pornography is an offence under section 15 of the Act and under the Information Technology Act, and recommended the expression 'child sexually abusive and exploitative material'. Article 15(3) permits special provision for women and children, Articles 39(e) and (f) direct the State to protect children from abuse and ensure opportunities for healthy development, and Article 21 includes dignity. Whether any provision has since been amended is a matter of the current statute.

questions.question: A touches the body of a ten-year-old through clothing, with sexual intent. On the passage, the offence of sexual assault

options.A: cannot be made out, because the clothing breaks the physical link between the accused and the child's body altogether
options.B: cannot be made out, because skin-to-skin contact is essential to the offence
options.C: can be made out, because Satish requires sexual intent and not direct skin-to-skin contact
options.D: can be made out only if penetration occurs, since mere touching with sexual intent amounts only to harassment of a child

questions.explanation: Satish holds that sexual intent is the test and skin-to-skin contact is not required.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B and Option A restate the overruled Bombay High Court view. Option D confuses sexual assault with penetrative assault.
questions.clat_trap: The overruled high court position is repeated in two options to look authoritative.
questions.language_trick: 'sexual intent' is the key phrase.

questions.question: On the passage, the effect of Independent Thought on the marital exception is that

options.A: the exception now covers a wife of fifteen years of age or above
options.B: the exception was struck down completely, so marital rape is an offence for all wives
options.C: the exception was upheld in full as a valid classification under Article 14
options.D: the exception protects only a wife aged eighteen or above

questions.explanation: The exception, as aligned after Independent Thought, protects only intercourse with a wife aged eighteen or above.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B overstates the holding. Option A states the earlier age. Option C reverses the outcome.
questions.clat_trap: The student may recall 'marital rape' and over-extend the holding; the Court read down the exception only as regards wives under eighteen.
questions.language_trick: 'only' limits the exception.

questions.question: Just Rights for Children Alliance is best summarised as holding that

options.A: storage is an offence under the Information Technology Act alone and not under POCSO, which deals only with actual abuse of children and not with material
options.B: only the creation and circulation of such material is an offence under section 15
options.C: storing or viewing such material, and not only sharing it, can be an offence, and the Court preferred a different label for the material
options.D: consensual viewing between adults of any age is punishable under section 15

questions.explanation: The Court held that storing or viewing is an offence under section 15 of POCSO and the IT Act and recommended a new expression.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B narrows the offence. Option A excludes POCSO. Option D misdescribes the context as adults.
questions.clat_trap: Creation and circulation are the familiar offences, so the student tends to limit the holding to them.
questions.language_trick: 'not only sharing' extends the offence.

questions.question: Article 15(3) is relevant to the Act because

options.A: it makes every provision for women exempt from Article 14 and judicial review
options.B: it permits special provision for children and women
options.C: it requires the State to treat boys and girls differently under every statute, whatever the context or the object
options.D: it requires the State to reserve seats for children in all educational institutions

questions.explanation: Article 15(3) is an enabling provision for special measures for women and children.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates the exemption. Option D confuses the Article with Article 15(5) and reservation. Option C makes differential treatment compulsory.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'special' in the Article attracts overstatement in the options.
questions.language_trick: 'permits' marks an enabling, not compulsory, provision.

questions.question: Under the passage, the presumption in section 29 of the Act

options.A: arises automatically on the filing of a complaint, without proof of any fact
options.B: removes the prosecution's duty to prove any fact at all in the case
options.C: operates only in cases of penetrative assault and never in cases of sexual assault or of the aggravated forms of either
options.D: arises once the foundational facts are established and places an evidentiary burden on the accused

questions.explanation: The passage says the presumption operates once the foundational facts are shown.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A drops the foundational facts. Option C limits the presumption wrongly. Option B overstates its effect.
questions.clat_trap: 'Presumption' suggests that nothing needs proof, which the passage corrects.
questions.language_trick: 'once the foundational facts are shown' is the condition.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A person who stores child sexually abusive material, without sharing it, can be prosecuted under the POCSO Act. Reason (R): Section 15 of the Act is confined to cases in which the material is shared or transmitted to others.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true on the passage, which says storing or viewing is an offence. R is false because the section is not confined to sharing.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R contradicts the passage and cannot explain A. A is true.
questions.clat_trap: Students who recall 'circulation' offences accept R and then choose a both-true option.
questions.language_trick: 'confined to' makes R an absolute restriction.

passages.title: Organised Crime, Terrorism and the Bail Bar: BNS ss.111-113, the UAPA and Article 22
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 introduced organised crime (section 111) and petty organised crime (section 112) as separate offences, and defined a terrorist act (section 113) as an act done with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security or economic security of India or to strike terror in people. Organised crime is continuing unlawful activity by a member of a syndicate, such as kidnapping, extortion or contract killing, undertaken for material benefit, and it carries imprisonment from five years to life, and death where a death results. Petty organised crime covers lesser group offences such as theft and snatching. The terrorist act overlaps with the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, whose section 43D(5) bars bail where the court finds the accusations prima facie true. In NIA v Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali (2019), the Court held that at the bail stage the court must look at the totality of the material but need not weigh evidence meticulously. In Union of India v K A Najeeb (2021), it held that section 43D(5) does not oust the power of constitutional courts to grant bail where long incarceration and delay in trial infringe Article 21. In Arup Bhuyan (2011), the Court read down the provision on membership of a banned organisation, holding that mere membership does not make a person criminally liable unless he resorts to violence or incites it. In Kartar Singh (1994), the Court upheld the TADA with safeguards while insisting that penal definitions must not be vague. In Prabir Purkayastha v State (NCT of Delhi) (2024), the Court held an arrest invalid where the grounds of arrest were not furnished to the accused in writing, as Article 22(1) requires. Article 19(4) permits reasonable restrictions on the freedom of association in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India.

questions.question: A syndicate has for several years run an extortion racket with violence, sharing the proceeds among its members. On the passage, the offence attracted is

options.A: organised crime under section 111, because the activity is continuing, syndicate-based and aimed at material benefit
options.B: petty organised crime under section 112, because group extortion falls in the lesser category
options.C: a terrorist act under section 113, because organised violence against citizens always threatens the security of the State
options.D: no offence under the Sanhita, because organised crime applies only where death has resulted

questions.explanation: The facts match the definition of organised crime: continuing unlawful activity by a syndicate for material benefit. Extortion is one of the examples named in the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats 'petty' as describing the size of the group, whereas it describes the lesser nature of the offences. Option C makes an absolute claim ('always') that the passage does not support. Option D confuses the death-penalty clause with the basic offence.
questions.clat_trap: The pair of sections 111 and 112 looks alike, and a student may choose the lighter one because extortion seems minor. The decisive words are 'continuing' and 'syndicate'.
questions.language_trick: 'petty' qualifies the offences (theft, snatching), not the gang; 'always' in the terrorist-act option is the overstatement.

questions.question: The decision in Najeeb means that the statutory bail bar in section 43D(5)

options.A: is struck down by the Court as violating Article 21 and no longer applies to any accused under the Act
options.B: cannot stop a constitutional court from granting bail after long delay
options.C: does not apply to accused persons who have already spent more than half of the maximum sentence in custody
options.D: applies with full force until the trial court finds that the delay is attributable to the prosecution and not to the accused

questions.explanation: Najeeb leaves the section on the statute book but holds that it does not oust the constitutional court's power to grant bail where prolonged incarceration and delay infringe Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A says the provision was struck down, which Najeeb did not do. Option D adds a requirement of attributing delay to the prosecution that the passage does not state. Option C invents a half-sentence threshold.
questions.clat_trap: A ruling that softens a bar is often remembered as a ruling that removes the bar. The correct option is also the shortest, so a student who prefers detailed options may skip it.
questions.language_trick: 'does not oust' is narrower than 'strikes down'; 'any accused' and 'no longer applies' signal overreach.

questions.question: A person is arrested under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and the arrest memo records no grounds, although the officer explained the facts orally at the time. On the passage, the arrest is

options.A: valid, because Article 22(1) applies only to preventive detention and not to arrest under penal statutes
options.B: open to being held invalid under Article 22(1), since the grounds were not furnished to him in writing, whatever was said to him orally
options.C: invalid only if he proves that he suffered real prejudice in his defence from the omission of written grounds
options.D: valid, because oral communication of the grounds by a senior officer satisfies the requirement of Article 22(1)

questions.explanation: Prabir Purkayastha holds that the grounds must be furnished in writing. Oral explanation does not cure the defect.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D accepts oral communication, which the Court rejected. Option A wrongly confines Article 22(1) to preventive detention. Option C adds a prejudice test the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The oral explanation looks like substantial compliance, which courts sometimes accept in other settings. The passage fixes writing as the form.
questions.language_trick: 'whatever was said orally' in the correct option closes the substantial-compliance route.

questions.question: X is a mere member of a banned organisation and has never used or incited violence. On the passage, a prosecution against him for membership alone

options.A: can be sustained, because Article 19(4) removes all protection of association from members of banned groups
options.B: can be sustained, because the ban on the organisation itself makes every member a presumed offender
options.C: cannot be sustained, since membership without resort to violence or incitement to it does not by itself make a person liable under the provision as read down
options.D: cannot be sustained, because Kartar Singh held that membership offences are void for vagueness in every case

questions.explanation: Arup Bhuyan reads down the membership provision so that violence or incitement is required.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns the ban into a presumption of guilt. Option A overreads Article 19(4), which permits only reasonable restrictions. Option D attributes to Kartar Singh a holding it did not make, and 'every case' is an overstatement.
questions.clat_trap: The right result (cannot be sustained) appears twice, so a hurried reader picks on outcome and misses the faulty reason.
questions.language_trick: Two options share the same outcome; the reasoning clause, not the outcome, decides.

questions.question: At the bail stage under section 43D(5), the passage says that the court

options.A: looks at the totality of material without weighing evidence meticulously
options.B: may grant bail on merits only after the investigating agency has completed its examination of every prosecution witness
options.C: must accept the prosecution's case as true and has no power to examine any material produced by the accused
options.D: must hold a mini-trial and test the credibility of each prosecution witness before deciding whether accusations are prima facie true

questions.explanation: Watali requires the court to look at the whole material but not to weigh it as at trial.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D converts bail into a trial. Option C removes any judicial scrutiny. Option B makes bail depend on completion of the investigation.
questions.clat_trap: Two extreme options sit on either side of the correct middle position, so the correct option looks bland.
questions.language_trick: 'meticulously' is the key adverb; the wrong options remove or exaggerate the scrutiny.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the passage. I. Petty organised crime covers lesser group offences such as theft and snatching. II. Organised crime can attract death where a death results. III. Under Najeeb, section 43D(5) must be applied without regard to the length of trial delay. IV. Prabir Purkayastha concerned the furnishing of grounds of arrest in writing. Which are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II and IV only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, II and IV restate the passage. Statement III is the opposite of Najeeb.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement III denies the Article 21 exception. Options containing III cannot be right.
questions.clat_trap: Statement III is a plausible-sounding reversal of Najeeb, placed among true statements to mislead a student who remembers 'bail bar' but not the exception.
questions.language_trick: 'must be applied without regard to' is an absolute formula.

passages.title: Speech-Linked Offences in the BNS: Enmity, Religious Feelings and Public Mischief
passages.passage: Three provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita carry forward offences that regulate speech. Section 196 punishes promoting enmity between groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language and similar grounds, and doing acts prejudicial to harmony; section 299 punishes deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage the religious feelings of a class by insulting its religion or beliefs; and section 353 punishes statements, rumours or reports conducing to public mischief. Each must satisfy Article 19(2), which permits reasonable restrictions on speech in the interests, among others, of public order, decency or morality and of preventing incitement to an offence. In Ramji Lal Modi v State of UP (1957), the Court upheld the predecessor of section 299 because it punished only aggravated forms of insult committed with deliberate and malicious intention, which have a tendency to disturb public order. In Kedar Nath Singh (1962), the Court read the sedition law to reach only acts with a tendency to create disorder or incite violence. In Ramesh v Union of India (1988), the effect of a speech was to be judged by the standards of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous men, not those of weak and vacillating minds. In Amish Devgan v Union of India (2020), the Court held that hate speech injures the dignity and the equal citizenship of the targeted group, and that the speaker's position and the context are relevant in judging its gravity. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Court distinguished mere discussion and advocacy, which are protected, from incitement, which is not. The expression 'public order' was inserted in Article 19(2) by the First Amendment of 1951, so that speech threatening public tranquillity could be restricted even where it fell short of endangering the security of the State.

questions.question: A satirical essay mocks a religious practice but uses no abuse and makes no attempt to provoke any group. A prosecution under section 299 is

options.A: likely to succeed, because any statement that offends the religious sentiments of a class is punishable under the section, whatever the speaker's intention or manner
options.B: unlikely to succeed, since the section needs deliberate and malicious intention to outrage religious feelings, which mere criticism lacks
options.C: likely to succeed, because the ground of decency in Article 19(2) removes protection from satire directed at religion
options.D: unlikely to succeed, because speech about religion lies wholly outside the reach of Article 19(2) restrictions

questions.explanation: Ramji Lal Modi saved the provision only because it punishes aggravated, deliberate and malicious insults. Criticism or satire without that intention falls outside it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A drops the intention requirement. Option C wrongly treats decency as a blanket ground against religious satire. Option D claims religion is outside Article 19(2) altogether, which is not true.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'offends' tempts students to equate offence with the offence. The Court limited the section to deliberate and malicious acts.
questions.language_trick: 'deliberate and malicious' are the narrowing words; 'any statement that offends' is the broad paraphrase.

questions.question: Applying the Ramesh standard, a court judging the effect of a speech on its audience should ask how it would affect

options.A: reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous people, not weak or vacillating ones, in context
options.B: the most sensitive member of the targeted community, since the section protects the weakest listener
options.C: the speaker's own audience only, ignoring how the speech spreads through publication and repetition
options.D: the average member of the majority community, since public order rests on majority reaction

questions.explanation: Ramesh fixes the standard as that of the reasonable, strong-minded person.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B picks the most sensitive listener, which Ramesh rejects. Option D brings in a majority-community test not found in the passage. Option C ignores the audience standard altogether.
questions.clat_trap: The most sensitive person looks like the natural beneficiary of a hate-speech rule, so option one is tempting.
questions.language_trick: 'weak and vacillating' in the passage is the excluded standard.

questions.question: According to Amish Devgan, hate speech is a wrong because

options.A: it undermines the sovereignty and integrity of the State, the only ground recognised for restricting such speech
options.B: it necessarily leads to physical violence against members of that group within a short period of the broadcast
options.C: it injures the dignity and equal citizenship of the targeted group
options.D: it offends the personal reputation of individual members of the group and is therefore a form of defamation

questions.explanation: The Court's reasoning is based on dignity and equal citizenship.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B adds a necessary link with violence, which the passage does not require. Option D treats it as defamation of individuals. Option A claims that sovereignty is the only ground, which the text of Article 19(2) contradicts.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is the shortest and sounds abstract, whereas the wrong ones sound concrete.
questions.language_trick: 'necessarily' and 'only' are overstatements.

questions.question: A speaker argues, in abstract terms and without urging anyone to act, that a particular law should be repealed. On the passage, the speech is

options.A: protected only if it is delivered in a public place before an audience that has been given prior notice of it
options.B: unprotected unless the speaker also shows that the impugned law is unconstitutional on its face
options.C: protected, since discussion or advocacy short of incitement lies outside the restrictions in Article 19(2)
options.D: unprotected, since any call to change a law has a tendency to disturb public order in a democratic society, however abstractly it is put

questions.explanation: Shreya Singhal protects discussion and advocacy; only incitement may be restricted.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D treats public order as triggered by any advocacy. Option B adds a burden to prove unconstitutionality. Option A adds a prior-notice condition that is absent.
questions.clat_trap: Public order is a familiar ground and tempts students to restrict. The passage draws the line at incitement.
questions.language_trick: 'abstract' and 'without urging' show that incitement is missing.

questions.question: The insertion of 'public order' in Article 19(2) is relevant because it

options.A: allowed speech to be restricted where it threatens public tranquillity, even short of endangering the security of the State
options.B: extended the application of Article 19(2) to private persons and corporations who speak in public places
options.C: made incitement to an offence the only ground on which hate speech may be punished under the Sanhita
options.D: removed the requirement that restrictions on speech be reasonable, leaving their necessity to Parliament alone, so that courts could no longer review them

questions.explanation: The passage says public order allows restriction short of a threat to State security.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D claims the reasonableness test was dropped, which is not stated. Option C treats incitement as the only ground, which contradicts the list in Article 19(2). Option B invents horizontal application.
questions.clat_trap: Students recall that the First Amendment was controversial and attribute to it broader effects than the passage states.
questions.language_trick: 'short of' in the correct option marks the gap between public order and State security.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Section 353 of the Sanhita must also satisfy the test of Article 19(2) to be valid. Reason (R): Ramji Lal Modi upheld the predecessor of section 299 only because it punished aggravated forms of insult committed deliberately and maliciously.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Assertion A is true, as the passage says each provision must satisfy Article 19(2). Reason R is also true, but it concerns section 299 and its safeguards and does not explain why section 353 must satisfy Article 19(2).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a true fact about a different provision and does not explain A.
questions.clat_trap: Two true statements sit together and a student assumes that they are connected because both concern speech offences. R is about section 299, A about section 353.
questions.language_trick: 'also' in A links to Article 19(2), not to Ramji Lal Modi.

passages.subject_area: Special Criminal Laws and Constitutional Law
passages.title: PMLA, the Twin Conditions and Constitutional Safeguards
passages.passage: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 makes it an offence to be involved in any process connected with proceeds of crime, which are property derived from a scheduled offence. The Directorate of Enforcement may summon persons and record statements (section 50), attach property (section 5) and arrest where it has reason to believe, recorded in writing, that a person is guilty (section 19). Section 45 requires, for bail, that the court be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit an offence while on bail. In Nikesh Tarachand Shah v Union of India (2017), an earlier version of the twin conditions was struck down; Parliament re-enacted the conditions in 2018. In Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v Union of India (2022), a three-judge Bench upheld the main provisions, holding that an Enforcement Case Information Report is an internal document and not an FIR, and that statements recorded under section 50 are not barred by Article 20(3) where the person was not then an accused (review proceedings: verify current status). In Pankaj Bansal v Union of India (2023), the Court held that grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing. In Tarun Kumar v Directorate of Enforcement (2023), it held that there can be no money laundering without proceeds of crime. In V Senthil Balaji (2024), the Court granted bail relying on Article 21 and prolonged incarceration. In Manish Sisodia (2024), the Court said that bail is the rule even under the PMLA where trial is delayed.

questions.question: The Enforcement Directorate arrests X on a charge of laundering, but the scheduled offence's FIR is quashed and no property derived from it can be shown. On the passage, the PMLA case

options.A: cannot stand, because the ECIR is no FIR
options.B: stands, because the Directorate's recorded reason to believe is sufficient to continue the prosecution
options.C: stands, because laundering is an independent offence that needs no link to any scheduled offence at all
options.D: cannot stand, as without proceeds of crime there can be no offence of money laundering at all

questions.explanation: Tarun Kumar holds that without proceeds of crime there is no money laundering. Quashing of the scheduled offence leaves nothing to launder.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C denies the dependence on a scheduled offence. Option B confuses the arrest standard with the existence of the offence. Option A contradicts Madanlal, which says an ECIR is not an FIR.
questions.clat_trap: Students recall that money laundering is described as 'standalone' and overlook that the proceeds must derive from a scheduled offence.
questions.language_trick: 'independent' in the first wrong option is partly true but incomplete.

questions.question: An accused argues that he was not given a copy of the ECIR before arrest. On the passage, the argument is

options.A: strong, because Madanlal held that arrest without supply of the ECIR violates Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India
options.B: weak, since an ECIR is an internal document and not an FIR, although grounds of arrest must be given in writing
options.C: strong, since the ECIR stands on the same footing as an FIR and must be furnished to every person arrested
options.D: weak, since Article 22(1) does not apply to arrests made by the Directorate under this Act at all

questions.explanation: Madanlal treats the ECIR as an internal document, but Pankaj Bansal requires written grounds of arrest.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C equates ECIR and FIR. Option D wrongly excludes Article 22(1). Option A attributes to Madanlal a holding it did not make.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is a two-part answer: the ECIR need not be supplied but grounds must be.
questions.language_trick: 'although' joins the two strands; wrong options pick one strand only.

questions.question: Statements recorded under section 50 attract the protection of Article 20(3) only if

options.A: the statement relates to an offence in which the Directorate has also attached property of the person
options.B: the statement is recorded in the presence of a lawyer chosen by the person summoned and is later signed by him
options.C: the summons is issued after the Directorate has received the report of the investigating officer on the scheduled offence
options.D: the person was an accused when the statement was made

questions.explanation: Madanlal says Article 20(3) is not attracted where the person was not then an accused.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B adds a lawyer-presence condition. Option A ties the protection to attachment. Option C ties it to receipt of a police report.
questions.clat_trap: 'only if' invites a search for the narrowest condition, and the short correct option looks incomplete.
questions.language_trick: 'then an accused' fixes the time of the statement.

questions.question: The observation in Manish Sisodia means, on the passage, that

options.A: the twin conditions in section 45 stand repealed for all accused detained for more than a year
options.B: delay in trial can outweigh the twin conditions
options.C: bail must be granted to every accused who has spent more than six months in custody pending trial
options.D: the court may ignore the gravity of the allegations while considering bail under the Act

questions.explanation: The observation links delay and Article 21 to bail even under the PMLA, without removing the conditions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A claims repeal. Option C invents a six-month rule. Option D treats gravity as irrelevant.
questions.clat_trap: 'bail is the rule' is often read as an unconditional entitlement.
questions.language_trick: 'even under' signals an exception to a stricter regime, not a repeal.

questions.question: Parliament's re-enactment of the twin conditions in 2018, after Nikesh Tarachand Shah, illustrates that

options.A: a legislature may not re-enact any provision that has been struck down, however it is revised or reasoned afresh
options.B: a legislature may cure the defect found by the Court and re-enact the provision in a corrected form
options.C: the decision was prospective only and left earlier bail orders untouched by any later amendment of the Act
options.D: the Court's decision was overruled by the amending Act, which restored the earlier text

questions.explanation: A statute struck down for a defect may be re-enacted after the defect is removed. The passage says Parliament re-enacted the conditions in 2018.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a bar that does not exist. Option D confuses legislative cure with overruling, since only a court can overrule a judgment. Option C invents a prospective-only holding.
questions.clat_trap: 'overruled by the amending Act' is a standard trap: legislation does not overrule a judgment but removes its basis.
questions.language_trick: 'overruled' is a judicial term.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the passage. I. An ECIR is an internal document and not an FIR. II. Grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing. III. The twin conditions of section 45 were upheld in Nikesh Tarachand Shah. IV. The review of Madanlal has been finally decided by a larger Bench. Which are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: I and II only
options.D: I, II and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and II restate the passage. Statement III reverses Nikesh Tarachand Shah, which struck the earlier conditions down. Statement IV is unsupported, as the passage says to verify the status of review.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: III and IV are false and cannot appear in a correct combination.
questions.clat_trap: Statement III reverses a holding and IV states as final what the passage marks as to be verified.
questions.language_trick: 'finally decided' is the unsupported assertion.

passages.subject_area: Special Criminal Laws and Constitutional Law
passages.title: Juvenile Justice: Heinous Offences, Age and Criminal Responsibility
passages.passage: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 defines a child as a person below eighteen. Offences are classed as petty (maximum up to three years), serious (three to seven years) and heinous (a minimum punishment of seven years or more). A child between sixteen and eighteen alleged to have committed a heinous offence may be tried as an adult only after a preliminary assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board of his mental and physical capacity to commit the offence, his ability to understand its consequences and the circumstances in which he allegedly committed it. In Shilpa Mittal v State of NCT of Delhi (2020), the Court held that an offence whose maximum punishment exceeds seven years but which prescribes no minimum is a serious offence, not a heinous one, unless the statute provides a minimum of seven years. In Salil Bali v Union of India (2013), the Court upheld eighteen as the age of juvenility. In Pratap Singh v State of Jharkhand (2005), a Constitution Bench held that the date of the offence, not of the trial, decides juvenility. In Hari Ram v State of Rajasthan (2009), the Court held that the Act overrides other laws in determining age. In Mukarrab v State of UP (2017), the Court held that documentary evidence of age takes priority and that medical ossification tests are only a last resort. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 treats a child under seven as incapable of crime and a child between seven and twelve as immune where he lacks maturity of understanding. The Constitution supports special treatment through Articles 15(3), 21, 39(e) and (f).

questions.question: A seventeen-year-old is alleged to have committed an offence punishable with a maximum of ten years and no minimum. On the passage, the Board should

options.A: treat it as heinous because the maximum exceeds seven years, and conduct a preliminary assessment
options.B: treat it as a serious offence, so that the route of preliminary assessment for transfer to adult trial reserved for heinous offences is not available
options.C: treat it as petty because no minimum punishment is prescribed for the offence
options.D: refer him automatically to the Children's Court because he is above sixteen years of age

questions.explanation: Shilpa Mittal classifies such an offence as serious, not heinous, so the adult-trial route does not open.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A equates a high maximum with heinousness. Option C reads the absence of a minimum as pettiness. Option D ignores the requirement of assessment.
questions.clat_trap: The ten-year maximum looks heinous; the passage's test is the minimum of seven years.
questions.language_trick: 'minimum' versus 'maximum' is the language trick.

questions.question: A boy aged seventeen at the time of the offence is tried only when he is twenty. On the passage, the relevant date for juvenility is

options.A: the date of the offence, so that he is treated as a child
options.B: the date of the trial, so that he is treated as an adult
options.C: the date of framing of charge, which fixes juvenility for the whole proceeding
options.D: the date on which the Board receives the police report on the offence

questions.explanation: Pratap Singh holds that the date of the offence decides juvenility.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B adopts the trial date. Option C and Option D invent other dates.
questions.clat_trap: Delay in trial often makes an accused an adult by the time of trial, and a student may mark the trial date.
questions.language_trick: 'at the time of the offence' in the stem.

questions.question: On the passage, in determining the age of a person claiming juvenility,

options.A: the statement of the parents prevails over any school record or birth certificate produced before the Board
options.B: the Board must obtain a bone-age report in every case before it examines any document of age
options.C: a medical ossification test is the primary evidence and documents only corroborate it where it is inconclusive
options.D: documents come first and ossification is a last resort

questions.explanation: Mukarrab gives priority to documents and relegates medical tests to a last resort.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C reverses the order. Option A gives priority to the parents' statement. Option B makes medical tests mandatory.
questions.clat_trap: Medical evidence sounds scientific and objective, which tempts students to choose it first.
questions.language_trick: 'last resort' marks the rank order.

questions.question: A child aged ten commits an act which would be an offence. Under the BNS as described, he

options.A: is absolutely immune because he is below twelve, whatever his maturity of understanding
options.B: is liable unless the Board declares in writing that he is below the age of criminal responsibility
options.C: is liable as an adult for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment only
options.D: is immune only if he lacks maturity to judge its nature and consequences

questions.explanation: Between seven and twelve, immunity depends on lack of maturity of understanding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives absolute immunity to a child below twelve, which applies only below seven. Option C imports an adult-liability rule. Option B invents a written declaration.
questions.clat_trap: The seven and twelve thresholds are easily merged, and 'absolute' is attractive for a young child.
questions.language_trick: 'only if' and 'lacks maturity' are the operative phrases.

questions.question: The reference to Articles 15(3), 21, 39(e) and (f) supports the argument that

options.A: classification of children for special treatment is valid only if all persons below eighteen are treated identically
options.B: the State may design a separate, protective and reformative process for children, a classification consistent with equality because children differ from adults in capacity
options.C: children cannot be punished for any offence because Article 21 guarantees an absolute right to liberty
options.D: Article 15(3) forbids any distinction between children and adults in matters of criminal procedure

questions.explanation: Articles 15(3), 39(e) and (f) support special provisions for children, and the age classification rests on an intelligible differentia.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C turns Article 21 into an absolute bar. Option A and Option D contradict the special-provision logic of Article 15(3).
questions.clat_trap: Equality arguments may seem to forbid special treatment, but Article 15(3) is a saving clause for children and women.
questions.language_trick: 'absolute' and 'forbids any' are extreme words.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Pratap Singh the date of trial decides whether an accused is a juvenile. Reason (R): Pratap Singh was decided by a Constitution Bench.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because the date of the offence, not of the trial, decides juvenility. R is true, as the passage records a Constitution Bench.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A reverses the holding while R states a fact correctly.
questions.clat_trap: The authority of a Constitution Bench makes a student assume the first statement is also correct.
questions.language_trick: 'date of trial' versus 'date of the offence'.

passages.title: BNSS: Arrest, Custody, Default Bail and Undertrial Release
passages.passage: Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 lets police arrest without warrant in specified situations, but for offences punishable up to seven years it requires, as a rule, a notice of appearance, reflecting the principle in Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014). Section 43 permits handcuffing only for specified categories such as habitual offenders, persons who have escaped from custody and those accused of organised crime, terrorism or drug offences (verify the list). Section 47 requires the grounds of arrest to be communicated, and Article 22(1) and (2) guarantee the right to be told the grounds, to consult a lawyer of choice and to be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours. Under section 187, police custody up to fifteen days may be authorised in the first forty or sixty days of the investigation period; if the investigation is not completed within sixty or ninety days, the accused acquires an indefeasible right to default bail, as held in Uday Mohanlal Acharya (2001) and Rakesh Kumar Paul (2017). The right is lost only if the accused fails to apply before the chargesheet is filed. Section 479 provides that an undertrial who has served one-third of the maximum sentence, if a first offender, or one-half in other cases, shall be released on bail; it does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment. In Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (2024), the Court urged jails to apply it to eligible undertrials (verify scope). In Satender Kumar Antil v CBI (2022), the Court classified offences for bail and urged a special law on bail. In Sushila Aggarwal (2020), the Court held that anticipatory bail is not automatically limited in time. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) locates speedy trial in Article 21.

questions.question: A is accused of an offence punishable with five years' imprisonment. On the passage, the ordinary course under section 35 is

options.A: to arrest him only if the offence is cognizable and has also been reported by an eyewitness
options.B: to seek a warrant from the Magistrate, since no arrest without warrant is permitted for such offences
options.C: to issue a notice of appearance rather than arrest
options.D: to arrest him at once and produce him before the Magistrate for remand within twenty-four hours

questions.explanation: For offences up to seven years, a notice of appearance is the rule, reflecting Arnesh Kumar.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D states the old practice of automatic arrest. Option B overstates by saying that no arrest without warrant is permitted. Option A adds an eyewitness condition.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is brief and may seem to omit an exception, but 'ordinary course' makes it complete.
questions.language_trick: 'as a rule' in the passage means exceptions exist but the ordinary course is notice.

questions.question: An undertrial, a first offender, is charged with an offence punishable with ten years and has spent four years in custody. Under section 479 as described,

options.A: he is entitled to release on bail, since one-third of the maximum is a little over three years and three months
options.B: he is not entitled, because he must first serve one-half of the maximum sentence prescribed
options.C: he is not entitled, because the section applies only to offences punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years
options.D: he is entitled only if the Magistrate finds that the investigation is complete and trial is not likely to end for some years yet

questions.explanation: A first offender qualifies after one-third of the maximum. One-third of ten years is about three years and four months, which he has crossed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies the one-half rule meant for others. Option C invents a seven-year limit. Option D adds conditions that the section does not impose.
questions.clat_trap: Students apply one-half by default, forgetting the first-offender concession.
questions.language_trick: 'first offender' selects the one-third rule.

questions.question: The ninety-day period for an offence punishable with life imprisonment expires with no chargesheet. The accused applies for bail on the ninety-first day, but before the Magistrate decides, the chargesheet is filed. On the passage, the right to default bail

options.A: is lost, because the filing of the chargesheet on the same day extinguishes it
