options.B: depends on the Magistrate's satisfaction that the accused is not likely to tamper with the evidence, and is not automatic
options.C: survives the late filing, because the right accrued on expiry of the period and the accused had applied for it before the chargesheet was filed
options.D: is lost, because default bail is available only if the delay is attributable to the prosecution

questions.explanation: The right accrues on expiry and is lost only if the accused fails to apply before the chargesheet is filed. Here he applied before.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the order of application and filing. Option D adds a fault requirement. Option B imports a discretionary test inconsistent with an indefeasible right.
questions.clat_trap: A late chargesheet seems to defeat the claim. The passage makes the order of application and filing decisive.
questions.language_trick: 'only if the accused fails to apply before' fixes the sequence.

questions.question: On the passage, an order granting anticipatory bail

options.A: does not lapse automatically after a fixed period
options.B: lapses when the chargesheet is filed unless the Sessions Court extends it by a reasoned order
options.C: must be limited to the period fixed by the court when granting it, usually thirty days at most
options.D: can be granted only after the accused has been summoned and has surrendered before the Magistrate

questions.explanation: Sushila Aggarwal holds that anticipatory bail is not automatically limited in time.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B and Option C impose time limits that the Court rejected. Option D adds a surrender requirement which defeats the purpose.
questions.clat_trap: Time-bound anticipatory bail was a common view in earlier decisions, so options with a time limit appear familiar.
questions.language_trick: 'automatically' is the key adverb in the passage.

questions.question: A first-time accused of simple hurt is handcuffed by police while being taken to court. On the passage, the handcuffing is

options.A: prohibited absolutely, because Article 22 bars handcuffing of every arrested person in all cases
options.B: permitted, because simple hurt is a cognizable offence and cognizable offences are listed in section 43
options.C: permitted, because section 43 allows handcuffing of any arrested person at the officer's discretion
options.D: outside the categories in section 43, which name habitual offenders, escapees and persons accused of organised crime, terrorism or drug offences, so it is open to challenge

questions.explanation: Section 43 permits handcuffing only for specified categories. A first-time accused of simple hurt is not within them.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C treats the power as general. Option B invents a list based on cognizability. Option A overstates Article 22 as an absolute bar.
questions.clat_trap: The new provision is narrow, and a student who assumes police discretion marks the first option.
questions.language_trick: 'only for specified categories' in the passage is the key restriction.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the passage. I. Section 35 requires notice of appearance as a rule for offences punishable up to seven years. II. Section 479 applies to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment. III. Default bail was recognised in Uday Mohanlal Acharya and Rakesh Kumar Paul. IV. Article 22(2) requires production before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours. Which are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: I, II and III only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, III and IV restate the passage. Statement II is false because section 479 does not apply to such offences.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Any option with II is wrong.
questions.clat_trap: Statement II reverses the exclusion in section 479 and sits among true statements.
questions.language_trick: 'applies to' versus 'does not apply to'.

passages.subject_area: Law of Evidence and Constitutional Law
passages.title: Confessions, Discovery and the Right against Self-Incrimination
passages.passage: Under evidence law, a confession made to a police officer is inadmissible against the accused, and a confession made while in police custody is inadmissible unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. A proviso allows so much of a statement made in custody as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered to be proved, whether or not it amounts to a confession. The Privy Council in Pulukuri Kottaya v King-Emperor (1947) held that only the part of the statement that is the immediate cause of the discovery is admissible, not the whole narrative. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 retains these rules in substance. In Aghnoo Nagesia v State of Bihar (1966), the Supreme Court held that a First Information Report that contains a confession cannot be used against its maker, because the report is made to a police officer. Article 20(3) of the Constitution provides that no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. In Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), the Court held that the bar covers testimonial compulsion, not the giving of specimen signatures or fingerprints. In Nandini Satpathy (1978) the Court extended the right to silence to the stage of investigation, and in Selvi (2010) it held that narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests cannot be administered without consent. In Toofan Singh v State of Tamil Nadu (2020), a Constitution Bench held that officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau are police officers for the purpose of the evidence rule, so that statements made to them under the NDPS Act are not admissible as confessions. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 additionally requires audio-video recording of the search and seizure process.

questions.question: A suspect in police custody tells the investigating officer, 'I hid the knife under the bridge, and I killed him.' The knife is then recovered from under the bridge. Under the passage, what may be proved against him?

options.A: The entire statement, because the proviso makes admissible everything said before a discovery is made
options.B: The entire statement, because the recovery of the knife confirms that the confession was true
options.C: Only the part relating distinctly to the knife's location
options.D: Nothing at all, because any statement made to a police officer in custody is wholly inadmissible

questions.explanation: The proviso admits only that part of the statement which relates distinctly to the fact discovered, here the place where the knife was hidden. The admission of killing remains inadmissible.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats the recovery as validating the confession, which the proviso does not do. Option D ignores the proviso altogether. Option A stretches the proviso to the whole narrative, contrary to Pulukuri Kottaya.
questions.clat_trap: The recovery of the knife tempts the reader to treat the whole statement as reliable, but the proviso is about the information that distinctly causes the discovery, not about truth of the rest.
questions.language_trick: 'relates distinctly' confines admissibility to the discovery-causing part.

questions.question: An accused himself lodges an FIR stating, 'I stabbed him in a quarrel.' The prosecution seeks to use the report against him. On the passage

options.A: it cannot be used as a confession against him, since it was made to a police officer
options.B: it can be used against him only if he was not in custody when he lodged the report with the officer in charge
options.C: it can be used against him, because a person who voluntarily reports a crime waives the protection of the evidence rule on confessions made to police officers
options.D: it is inadmissible only if it was made under threat

questions.explanation: Following Aghnoo Nagesia, an FIR that contains a confession cannot be used against its maker as a confession, since it is made to a police officer.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C invents a waiver by voluntary reporting. Option B confuses the custody limb of the rule with the limb on confessions to police officers. Option D makes admissibility depend on threat, which the rule does not.
questions.clat_trap: Voluntariness suggests admissibility, but the bar attaches to the person who receives the statement, not to whether the maker was pressured.
questions.language_trick: 'to a police officer' shows that the recipient, not the maker's will, triggers the bar.

questions.question: An accused of forgery is directed by a court to give specimen handwriting for comparison. He refuses, citing Article 20(3). On the passage, the refusal is

options.A: protected, because handwriting reflects personal knowledge
options.B: not protected, since specimen handwriting is physical evidence and not testimonial compulsion
options.C: protected, because any direction obliging an accused to participate in the investigation violates his right against being compelled to give testimony
options.D: protected, because Nandini Satpathy extends the right to silence to every direction issued during the investigation stage

questions.explanation: Kathi Kalu Oghad distinguishes testimonial compulsion from furnishing physical evidence such as specimen writing or fingerprints, which Article 20(3) does not bar.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C treats all participation as testimony. Option D stretches Nandini Satpathy, which concerns the right to remain silent in answering questions, to physical samples. Option A wrongly equates handwriting with conveying personal knowledge.
questions.clat_trap: The expansion of the right to silence in Nandini Satpathy tempts the reader to extend it to samples, but Kathi Kalu Oghad draws the line at testimony.
questions.language_trick: 'testimonial' is the operative word; physical samples are outside it.

questions.question: A person arrested by a Narcotics Control Bureau officer makes a statement under the NDPS Act admitting possession. At trial the prosecution relies on it as his confession. On Toofan Singh as described

options.A: the statement is admissible only after the court holds a trial within a trial on voluntariness
options.B: the statement is admissible, because NCB officers are not police officers
options.C: the statement is not admissible as a confession, because the officer is treated as a police officer for the evidence rule
options.D: the statement is admissible, because a special statute with its own investigative machinery displaces the general evidence rule on confessions made to police officers

questions.explanation: The Constitution Bench held that NCB officers are police officers for the evidence rule, so such statements are not admissible as confessions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D claims that the special statute displaces the evidence rule, which the Bench rejected. Option B states the opposite of the holding. Option A invents a voluntariness inquiry that would not cure the bar.
questions.clat_trap: A special statute with its own machinery sounds like it would override the general rule, which is the trap in the stem.
questions.language_trick: 'police officers for the purpose of the evidence rule' limits the holding to admissibility of confessions.

questions.question: An accused gives written consent, in the presence of his lawyer, to a polygraph test, and the result is offered at trial. On the passage, the best view is that

options.A: the result is inadmissible because the test was conducted in custody
options.B: the result is admissible only if the Magistrate attended the test
options.C: the test is hit by Article 20(3) regardless of consent, because the right against self-incrimination cannot be waived by an accused person
options.D: the test is not hit by Article 20(3), since the passage bars such tests only when administered without consent

questions.explanation: Selvi bars narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests when administered without consent. A voluntary test is not compelled.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C makes the right unwaivable, which the passage does not say. Option A and Option B add conditions not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The absolute-sounding first wrong option appeals to those who remember Selvi as a blanket prohibition.
questions.language_trick: 'without consent' qualifies the bar.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A statement made by an accused in police custody that leads to the discovery of a hidden weapon may be proved in part. Reason (R): Article 20(3) forbids the use of every statement made by an accused person while in police custody.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true, because the proviso admits the part that relates distinctly to the discovery. R is false, because Article 20(3) bars compulsion to give testimony, not every custodial statement, and the evidence rules operate separately.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A follows the proviso as described. R overstates Article 20(3), which is limited to compulsion.
questions.clat_trap: R sounds like a natural constitutional gloss and tempts a reader to pick the explanation option.
questions.language_trick: 'every statement' in R is an overstatement.

passages.title: Preventive Detention under Article 22 and the Limits of Executive Satisfaction
passages.passage: Article 22 of the Constitution deals with both punitive and preventive detention. Clauses (1) and (2) apply to persons arrested under ordinary criminal law and require that the person be told the grounds of arrest, be allowed to consult a lawyer of choice, and be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours. Clauses (3) to (7) permit preventive detention, which operates without trial and on the subjective satisfaction of the executive. Detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board, and the detainee must be informed of the grounds as soon as possible and given the earliest opportunity to make a representation. The Forty-fourth Amendment sought to reduce the period to two months and to restructure the Advisory Board, but the change has not been brought into force. Statutes such as the National Security Act, 1980 and the COFEPOSA operate within this framework. In A. K. Gopalan v State of Madras (1950) the Court read Article 22 as a self-contained code, but Maneka Gandhi (1978) later required that any law depriving personal liberty satisfy Articles 14, 19 and 21 as well. In Rekha v State of Tamil Nadu (2011), the Court said that preventive detention cannot be used merely to circumvent the grant of bail in an ordinary criminal case. In Banka Sneha Sheela v State of Telangana (2021) it held that disturbance of law and order does not by itself amount to disturbance of public order, so that detention for ordinary offences is unjustified. In Ameena Begum v State of Telangana (2023), the Court stressed that detention must be reasoned and cannot replace the ordinary criminal process. In Sama Aruna v State of Telangana (2018) it held that the grounds of detention must be communicated in a language the detainee understands.

questions.question: Which of the following distinguishes Article 22(1)-(2) from Article 22(3)-(7)?

options.A: The first applies to persons arrested for offences, the second to detention without trial
options.B: The first permits detention without production before a Magistrate, whereas the second requires production within twenty-four hours
options.C: The first requires an Advisory Board opinion, whereas the second requires only a written order of the executive
options.D: The first applies after conviction, whereas the second applies only to detainees awaiting trial

questions.explanation: Clauses (1) and (2) govern arrests under ordinary criminal law, with grounds, counsel and production before a Magistrate. Clauses (3) to (7) permit preventive detention without trial.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the safeguards. Option D wrongly ties the first set to conviction. Option C reverses the Advisory Board requirement.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option borrows a real feature of Article 22 but attaches it to the wrong set of clauses.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A person granted bail in a pending theft case is detained under a State preventive detention law. The only ground cited is the pending case. On Rekha and Banka Sneha Sheela

options.A: the detention is valid, as bail does not bind the executive
options.B: the detention is valid, because the executive's subjective satisfaction is conclusive and courts cannot examine whether the ground is relevant to public order
options.C: the detention is liable to be set aside, as it appears a device to defeat bail for an ordinary offence
options.D: the detention is valid, since a pending criminal case always shows a continuing threat to the maintenance of public order

questions.explanation: Rekha bars the use of preventive detention to circumvent bail, and Banka Sneha Sheela separates law and order from public order. A single pending ordinary case does not justify detention.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B makes satisfaction conclusive, ignoring judicial review. Option D uses 'always', which the cases reject. Option A ignores the bar on circumventing bail.
questions.clat_trap: The phrase 'subjective satisfaction' lures the reader into thinking courts cannot review, but review for relevance and purpose remains.
questions.language_trick: 'only ground cited' signals that nothing links the detainee to public order.

questions.question: A detainee who knows only Telugu is served with grounds of detention written in English without translation. On Sama Aruna

options.A: the detention is void, but only if the detainee proves prejudice from the absence of translation
options.B: the detention stands, because the Advisory Board will examine the grounds before the three-month period ends
options.C: the detention is vulnerable, because the grounds were not communicated in a language the detainee understands, defeating his right to make an effective representation
options.D: the detention stands, since Article 22(5) requires only that grounds be communicated, in any language

questions.explanation: Sama Aruna requires grounds in a language the detainee understands, because the right to make a representation is otherwise illusory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reads the requirement too thinly. Option B assumes the later Board cures the defect. Option A adds a prejudice requirement not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The reader who remembers only that grounds must be communicated may miss the qualifier on language.
questions.language_trick: 'in a language the detainee understands' is the specific qualifier.

questions.question: The Forty-fourth Amendment provisions on Article 22 described in the passage

options.A: are not yet operative, because the Amendment has not been brought into force
options.B: apply to detentions under the National Security Act, 1980 alone, since the later law was enacted with that Amendment in view
options.C: were struck down in Maneka Gandhi
options.D: apply to every detention, since an amendment operates from enactment

questions.explanation: The passage says the change to two months and the restructured Board has not been brought into force, so the three-month rule continues.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ties the change to one statute without basis. Option D treats an unenforced amendment as operative. Option C attributes a decision to Maneka Gandhi that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: An amendment that is passed but not notified is not law in operation, which students sometimes forget.
questions.language_trick: 'sought to' and 'has not been brought into force' control the answer.

questions.question: In what respect did Maneka Gandhi alter the reading of Article 22 found in Gopalan?

options.A: It reduced the maximum detention to two months
options.B: It required that a law authorising detention also satisfy Articles 14, 19 and 21, not Article 22 alone
options.C: It held that Article 22 applies to preventive detention only after the Advisory Board has confirmed the order
options.D: It struck down all preventive detention laws as inconsistent with Article 21, leaving only punitive detention valid

questions.explanation: Gopalan treated Article 22 as a self-contained code. Maneka Gandhi required that such a law also meet the tests under Articles 14, 19 and 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D overstates the holding to a total invalidation. Option C invents a sequence. Option A confuses the case with the unenforced Amendment.
questions.clat_trap: The reduction to two months belongs to the Forty-fourth Amendment, so the third option mixes two sources.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct on the passage? I. A detainee's grounds must be communicated in a language he understands. II. Detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board. III. Preventive detention may be used to avoid the grant of bail in ordinary criminal cases. IV. Disturbance of law and order always amounts to disturbance of public order.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: III and IV only
options.D: I, II and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and II restate the passage. III reverses Rekha. IV reverses Banka Sneha Sheela, which separates the two concepts.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: III and IV are contradicted by the cases cited in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Each false statement is the reverse of a holding, which a hurried reader may accept as plausible.
questions.language_trick: 'always' in IV signals the overstatement.

passages.title: Victim Justice, Compensation and Restorative Approaches
passages.passage: Victimology studies the role of the victim in crime. Mendelsohn and von Hentig argued that victims may contribute to their own victimisation through relationships or behaviour, an idea known as victim precipitation, though modern writing cautions against shifting blame. The United Nations Declaration of Basic Principles of Justice for Victims of Crime and Abuse of Power (1985) urges access to justice, fair treatment, restitution and compensation. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 allows a court to order the accused to pay compensation to the victim and requires every State to prepare a victim compensation scheme, with the scheme operating even where the accused is not traced or is acquitted. It also preserves the victim's right of appeal against an acquittal, a conviction for a lesser offence, or inadequate compensation. In Mallikarjun Kodagali v State of Karnataka (2018), the Supreme Court held that a victim has the right to appeal without having to obtain the leave of the High Court. In Jagjeet Singh v Ashish Mishra (2022), the Court held that the victim has a right to be heard at every stage, including at bail. On compounding, Gian Singh v State of Punjab (2012) held that the High Court may quash proceedings for non-compoundable offences on the basis of a settlement, except for heinous offences such as murder and rape and offences against society, a principle refined in Narinder Singh v State of Punjab (2014). Restorative justice, in contrast with retribution, focuses on repairing harm through dialogue between offender and victim, and mediation is increasingly used. Articles 21 and 39A of the Constitution supply the constitutional basis for fair treatment of victims and access to legal aid.

questions.question: A High Court is asked to quash proceedings for simple hurt in a neighbourhood quarrel after the parties settle, and also proceedings for rape in a case where the parties claim to have settled. On Gian Singh as described, the High Court

options.A: may quash both, since a genuine settlement between the parties is enough for any non-compoundable offence
options.B: must refuse both, since non-compoundable offences can never be disposed of on a settlement
options.C: may quash the rape case but not the hurt case, since the injury in the latter is physical
options.D: may consider quashing the hurt case on the settlement, but should decline in the rape case because heinous offences affect society beyond the parties

questions.explanation: Gian Singh allows quashing of non-compoundable offences on settlement but excludes heinous offences such as murder and rape.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A removes the heinous-offence exception. Option B removes the power to quash altogether. Option C reverses the application.
questions.clat_trap: The temptation is to say that a settlement binds the court in both cases or in neither, ignoring the line drawn by the Court.
questions.language_trick: 'except for heinous offences' is the qualifier.

questions.question: An accused is acquitted of robbery. The victim wishes to challenge the acquittal. On Mallikarjun Kodagali

options.A: the victim may appeal only if the State agrees to appeal and the High Court first grants special leave to him
options.B: the victim may seek only revision, since the right of appeal belongs exclusively to the prosecuting State
options.C: the victim may only be heard when the State appeals
options.D: the victim may appeal against the acquittal without first obtaining leave from the High Court

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court held that a victim has a right of appeal without leave of the High Court.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B deny the independent right of appeal. Option C reduces the victim to a hearing role.
questions.clat_trap: Earlier practice required leave, so the reader who remembers the old position is led astray.
questions.language_trick: 'without having to obtain the leave' is the key phrase.

questions.question: A victim is not summoned when the accused applies for bail in a serious offence. On Jagjeet Singh v Ashish Mishra, the hearing is

options.A: valid, because the victim is a witness and not a party, and the prosecutor alone represents the public interest
options.B: open to challenge, since the victim has a right to be heard at every stage, including bail
options.C: valid, because bail is a purely executive matter
options.D: valid, as the right to be heard arises only at the stage of trial and sentencing, not earlier

questions.explanation: The Court held that the victim has a right to be heard at every stage including bail.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats the victim as a mere witness. Option D limits the right to later stages. Option C wrongly calls bail executive.
questions.clat_trap: The traditional view that the State alone speaks for the public is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'every stage' defeats the later-stage limitation.

questions.question: Which statement about restorative justice is consistent with the passage?

options.A: It treats victim precipitation as the basis for reducing punishment
options.B: It aims to repair harm through dialogue between offender and victim, rather than focusing on punishment alone
options.C: It is confined to compoundable offences under the Sanhita
options.D: It replaces criminal prosecution altogether by transferring every offence to mediation, as the 1985 Declaration requires

questions.explanation: The passage describes restorative justice as repairing harm through dialogue, in contrast with retribution.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D overstates and misattributes the Declaration. Option A confuses restorative justice with victimology. Option C invents a limit.
questions.clat_trap: 'altogether' and 'every' make the first wrong option an overstatement.
questions.language_trick: 'in contrast with retribution' fixes the meaning.

questions.question: Victim precipitation, as the passage presents the idea of Mendelsohn and von Hentig, is best understood as

options.A: a principle that exempts the accused from punishment
options.B: a doctrine confined to offences against property
options.C: a rule of the 1985 Declaration under which compensation is reduced where the victim contributed to the harm he suffered
options.D: a theory that victims may contribute to victimisation, though modern writing cautions against blaming victims

questions.explanation: The passage describes victim precipitation as a theory of victim contribution, cautioned against in modern writing.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C converts a theory into a rule of the Declaration. Option A and Option B are unsupported.
questions.clat_trap: A sociological theory is dressed up as a legal rule in the first wrong option.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A victim whose accused was acquitted cannot claim compensation under the State scheme, because compensation depends on conviction. Reason (R): The Sanhita's scheme operates even where the accused is not traced or is acquitted.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false, because the scheme operates despite acquittal. R is true and states exactly that.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R contradicts A.
questions.clat_trap: A sounds like ordinary common sense, so the reader may mark A as true.
questions.language_trick: 'depends on conviction' is the false claim.

passages.title: Schools of Criminology and Their Echoes in Indian Law
passages.passage: Criminology offers rival explanations of crime. The classical school, associated with Cesare Beccaria (On Crimes and Punishments, 1764) and Jeremy Bentham, assumes that persons are rational and choose crime after weighing pleasure and pain, so that punishment should be certain, prompt and proportionate. The positivist school began with Cesare Lombroso, whose L'uomo delinquente (1876) argued that some offenders are born criminals showing atavistic physical traits; this biological determinism is now discredited, but Enrico Ferri added social and economic causes and Raffaele Garofalo emphasised psychological abnormality. Emile Durkheim treated crime as a normal feature of society and linked rising deviance to anomie, the breakdown of norms. Robert Merton (1938) developed strain theory, in which individuals who accept cultural goals but lack legitimate means may turn to innovation, including crime. Edwin Sutherland (1939) introduced the term white-collar crime and the theory of differential association, under which criminal behaviour is learned in intimate groups. Howard Becker's labelling theory argues that deviance is created by social reaction, so that stigma may entrench offending. Indian law shows traces of these ideas. The Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 reflects reformative thinking by allowing release of first offenders on probation. The Santhanam Committee (1964), concerned with corruption in public life, influenced the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 introduces community service as a punishment and creates offences of organised crime.

questions.question: A sociologist argues that a young man with no job but strong cultural pressure to be financially successful turned to theft. Under the passage, the theory most apt is

options.A: Merton's strain theory, since legitimate means to the cultural goal were lacking
options.B: Sutherland's differential association, since the man learned theft in an intimate group that approved it
options.C: Becker's labelling theory
options.D: Lombroso's born criminal theory, since poverty is visible as an atavistic physical trait in persons of this class

questions.explanation: The stem describes accepted cultural goals without legitimate means, which is the setting for Merton's strain theory and innovation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D relies on discredited biological determinism. Option B invents a facts not in the stem. Option C concerns social reaction, which the stem does not describe.
questions.clat_trap: Poverty may seem to point to a biological or group-learning theory, but the stem is about the gap between goals and means.
questions.language_trick: 'accepts cultural goals but lacks legitimate means' is the signal phrase.

questions.question: A company director knowingly approves misleading accounts to inflate profits and is prosecuted. A scholar says that such conduct shows how ordinary corporate culture can teach people to violate the law. This is closest to

options.A: Merton's innovation, because the director had no access to any legitimate means of earning profit at all
options.B: Sutherland's work on white-collar crime and differential association, because the behaviour was learned in a respectable occupational group
options.C: Lombroso's atavism, because the director's physical traits would reveal a predisposition to fraud
options.D: Beccaria's classical view, because the director could not have weighed the risk of punishment

questions.explanation: Sutherland introduced white-collar crime and differential association, which explains learned conduct among respectable groups.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C relies on a discredited theory. Option A contradicts the facts, as the director had legitimate means. Option D contradicts the rational choice assumption.
questions.clat_trap: Every option names a real theory, so the reader must test it against the facts.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which school is associated with the idea that a person chooses crime after weighing pleasure and pain?

options.A: The labelling school, since Becker stressed the effect of social reaction on offenders
options.B: The sociological school, since Durkheim treated crime as normal in every society
options.C: The classical school of Beccaria and Bentham
options.D: The positivist school, since Lombroso studied offenders' physical traits scientifically

questions.explanation: The passage attributes rational choice and the pleasure-pain calculus to the classical school.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option B and Option A describe different schools whose focus is not rational choice.
questions.clat_trap: The explanations attached to the wrong options are true of those schools, which makes them tempting.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The passage describes Lombroso's biological determinism as

options.A: still the basis on which the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 selects probationers
options.B: accepted by Ferri as the sole cause of crime, with social causes rejected
options.C: the origin of strain theory, which Merton developed from it in 1938
options.D: discredited today, though it began the positivist school

questions.explanation: The passage says the determinism is now discredited, though Lombroso began the positivist school.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses Ferri's addition of social causes. Option A links the Act to a discredited theory. Option C invents a derivation.
questions.clat_trap: A true detail about positivism is mixed with a false attribution in each wrong option.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which feature of Indian law best matches the labelling theory's warning that stigma may entrench offending?

options.A: The creation of organised crime offences in the 2023 Sanhita, which punishes syndicates more heavily
options.B: The reliance on strict deterrence through certain and proportionate punishment
options.C: The influence of the Santhanam Committee on the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
options.D: The release of first offenders on probation under the 1958 Act, which avoids the stigma and association of imprisonment

questions.explanation: Probation is a reformative device that avoids imprisonment, which is the response suggested by labelling theory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A concerns harsher punishment. Option C concerns corruption control. Option B reflects the classical school.
questions.clat_trap: The reader must connect a theory with a statute by inference rather than recall.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct? I. Beccaria stressed that punishment should be certain, prompt and proportionate. II. Lombroso's biological determinism remains the accepted basis of the positivist school. III. Sutherland introduced the term white-collar crime. IV. Durkheim treated crime as a normal feature of society.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II, III and IV only
options.C: I, III and IV only
options.D: I, II and III only

questions.explanation: I, III and IV restate the passage. II is wrong because the determinism is discredited.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II contradicts the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Statement II appears in several options, so a single wrong inclusion changes the answer.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.title: The Principle of Legality: Feuerbach, Fuller, Hart and Dworkin
passages.passage: The principle of legality, expressed in the maxim nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege and associated with Paul Johann Anselm von Feuerbach, requires that conduct be defined as an offence, with its penalty, by a prior and clear law. Article 20(1) of the Constitution gives it partial expression by barring conviction under an ex post facto law and a penalty greater than that in force at the time of the offence, though a change in procedure may apply retrospectively. Article 21 requires that any procedure depriving liberty be fair, just and reasonable, as Maneka Gandhi (1978) held. A related doctrine of vagueness holds that a penal law so imprecise that people cannot know what is forbidden violates the guarantees of equality and freedom under the Constitution. In Shreya Singhal (2015) the Court struck down section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for vagueness, and in Kartar Singh v State of Punjab (1994) it insisted that definitions in the anti-terror law be read narrowly and precisely. Lon Fuller, in The Morality of Law (1964), listed eight desiderata of a legal system: generality, promulgation, non-retroactivity, clarity, consistency, possibility of compliance, constancy and congruence between declared rule and official action. H. L. A. Hart, in The Concept of Law, distinguished primary rules of obligation from secondary rules, including the rule of recognition, and accepted a minimum content of natural law. John Austin treated law as the command of a sovereign backed by sanction. Ronald Dworkin, criticising positivism, argued that law includes principles and is best understood as integrity. Concerns have been voiced that section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced sedition, uses broad terms such as subversive activities, and its validity is the subject of challenge (verify current status).

questions.question: A new statute makes it an offence to act in a manner prejudicial to the public good without defining the phrase, and applies to acts done last year. Which of Fuller's desiderata are most clearly breached?

options.A: Clarity and non-retroactivity, as the prohibition is imprecise and operates on past conduct
options.B: Constancy and possibility of compliance, since the rule changes too often to follow
options.C: Consistency alone, because two provisions conflict
options.D: Generality and promulgation, because the rule is addressed to named individuals and was never published

questions.explanation: The vague phrase breaches clarity and its application to past acts breaches non-retroactivity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option B and Option C assume facts the stem does not state.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option names a real desideratum, so the reader must match it with the stem's facts.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A law enacted in 2025 changes the court that tries offences, and applies to offences committed in 2023. The law is

options.A: barred by Article 20(1), because every retrospective criminal statute is prohibited by the clause
options.B: valid only if the new court is of higher rank than the court previously competent to try the offence
options.C: not barred by Article 20(1), as a change in procedure may apply retrospectively
options.D: barred, since a greater penalty than at the time of the offence is imposed on the accused

questions.explanation: Article 20(1) forbids ex post facto offences and enhanced penalties, not procedural change such as a change of forum.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads the clause too widely. Option D assumes a heavier penalty, which the stem does not state. Option B adds a condition not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The word retrospective suggests a bar, but the clause is narrower.
questions.language_trick: 'penalty greater' and 'ex post facto' define the bar.

questions.question: Hart's contribution in contrast with Austin's command theory is best described as

options.A: rejecting any minimum content of natural law and insisting that legal validity depends wholly on the sovereign's sanction and habitual obedience
options.B: arguing that law is best understood as integrity, being a body of principles that justify the practice
options.C: listing eight desiderata of legality, such as generality, clarity and congruence with official action
options.D: distinguishing primary from secondary rules, including the rule of recognition, rather than viewing law only as sovereign commands

questions.explanation: Hart distinguished primary and secondary rules, including the rule of recognition, and accepted a minimum content of natural law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses Hart's acceptance of minimum natural law. Option B describes Dworkin. Option C describes Fuller.
questions.clat_trap: Three thinkers are named in the passage, and each wrong option borrows from another.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which contrast is accurate on the passage?

options.A: Dworkin argued law includes principles, whereas Austin treated law as a sovereign's command backed by sanction
options.B: Hart denied that rules of recognition exist, whereas Dworkin accepted them as the test of validity in every legal system
options.C: Feuerbach defended retroactive penalties, unlike Fuller
options.D: Fuller argued law is the command of a sovereign, whereas Austin listed eight conditions for a legal system to be moral

questions.explanation: The accurate contrast is Dworkin's inclusion of principles against Austin's command theory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D swaps Fuller and Austin. Option B reverses Hart and misdescribes Dworkin. Option C reverses Feuerbach's position.
questions.clat_trap: Swapping authors' views is the commonest trap in jurisprudence questions.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The vagueness concern about section 152 would be most strongly supported by which precedent as described?

options.A: Maneka Gandhi, where Article 22 was held to be a complete code on personal liberty
options.B: Gopalan, where vagueness was first recognised
options.C: Kartar Singh, where the anti-terror statute was struck down wholly because of its definitions
options.D: Shreya Singhal, where a provision was struck for vagueness in penal language

questions.explanation: Shreya Singhal struck down section 66A for vagueness, which is the closest precedent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses Maneka Gandhi's holding. Option C misdescribes Kartar Singh, where definitions were read narrowly. Option B attributes vagueness to Gopalan.
questions.clat_trap: Cases on liberty are all named, but only one struck a penal provision for vagueness.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A law that increases the maximum punishment for an offence can be applied to an offence committed before it was enacted, because punishment is a procedural matter. Reason (R): Article 20(1) forbids a penalty greater than that in force at the time of the offence.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false, because a heavier penalty cannot be applied to earlier offences. R is true and shows why A fails.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R contradicts A.
questions.clat_trap: The passage's statement that procedure may apply retrospectively tempts the reader to treat punishment as procedure.
questions.language_trick: 'because punishment is a procedural matter' is the false claim.

passages.title: Dowry Death, Cruelty and the Domestic Violence Act: Section 80 BNS and Constitutional Safeguards
passages.passage: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 penalises giving, taking and demanding dowry and places on the person who took or abetted the taking of a gift the burden of showing that it was not dowry. Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita provides that where a woman dies by burns or bodily injury, or otherwise than under normal circumstances, within seven years of her marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives in connection with a demand for dowry, the death is a dowry death, punishable with imprisonment for not less than seven years which may extend to life. The words 'soon before her death' require a proximate and live link between the cruelty and the death. Section 85 punishes cruelty by a husband or his relatives with imprisonment up to three years and fine. The presumption of dowry death in the law of evidence, retained in substance by the new law, operates once the ingredients of dowry death are shown. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is a civil statute that provides protection, residence, monetary relief and custody orders. In Hiral P Harsora v Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016), the Supreme Court struck down the words 'adult male' in the definition of respondent as arbitrary under Article 14, so that women relatives may be proceeded against. In Satish Chander Ahuja v Sneha Ahuja (2020), the Court held that a shared household is not confined to premises owned or tenanted by the husband but includes any household where the woman has lived in a domestic relationship, overruling the narrower view in S R Batra v Taruna Batra (2007). In Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014), the Court held that arrest for cruelty under the old section 498A is not automatic and must satisfy the statutory grounds. In Sushil Kumar Sharma v Union of India (2005), the Court upheld section 498A despite allegations of misuse. Article 15(3) permits special provision for women, and Article 51A(e) makes renouncing practices derogatory to women's dignity a duty.

questions.question: A woman dies by hanging in the fifth year of her marriage. Her in-laws had demanded dowry and harassed her for it in the first year, but no demand or harassment is shown for the three years before her death. On the passage, a prosecution for dowry death

options.A: is likely to fail, because no cruelty is shown to have been live and proximate to the death, as the words 'soon before' demand
options.B: is likely to succeed, because death within seven years of marriage is conclusive of dowry death
options.C: is likely to fail, because dowry death applies only where the death has been caused by burns or bodily injury
options.D: is likely to succeed, because any dowry demand made at any time during the marriage satisfies the words 'soon before her death'

questions.explanation: The ingredients include cruelty or harassment soon before the death, and the passage says that this needs a proximate and live link. A stale demand from the first year does not supply it, and the presumption does not arise.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats the seven-year period as sufficient by itself. Option D reads 'soon before' as 'at any time'. Option C ignores that the section also covers death otherwise than under normal circumstances.
questions.clat_trap: The seven-year period and the old dowry demand are both true on the facts, which tempts the student to complete the test too early.
questions.language_trick: 'soon before her death' is a time-linked phrase and not a synonym for 'during the marriage'.

questions.question: The ratio of Hiral P Harsora, as described, is that

options.A: the remedies in the 2005 Act were declared void under Article 21 because the Act is civil and not penal in nature
options.B: a woman cannot be proceeded against under the 2005 Act and her liability lies only under the criminal provision on cruelty
options.C: the words 'adult male' in the definition of respondent were arbitrary under Article 14, because protection of the woman does not depend on the sex of the person inflicting domestic violence
options.D: the definition of respondent was read down to include only the female relatives of the husband and not other persons

questions.explanation: The Court removed the words 'adult male' as arbitrary, which allows women relatives to be respondents.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the holding. Option D invents a reading down to female relatives only. Option A misuses Article 21 and the civil nature of the Act.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options use the right vocabulary (respondent, definition, Article 21) with the wrong holding.
questions.language_trick: 'struck down' differs from 'read down' and the passage uses the former.

questions.question: A woman lived after marriage in a house owned by her father-in-law, where she and her husband resided together. On Satish Chander Ahuja, the house

options.A: cannot be a shared household, since only premises owned or tenanted by the husband fall within the expression
options.B: is a shared household only after a civil court has declared her right of residence in it
options.C: is a shared household only if the husband also holds a share in it as a co-owner with the father-in-law
options.D: can be a shared household, as the husband need not own or rent it

questions.explanation: The Court rejected the narrow reading and held that a household in which the woman lived in a domestic relationship can be a shared household.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the overruled view of Batra. Option C adds a co-ownership condition. Option B adds a prior declaration that the Act does not need.
questions.clat_trap: The overruled view is stated as a fresh option, so a student who remembers only the name of the case may choose it.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A police officer arrests a husband on a complaint of cruelty solely because the offence is cognizable. On Arnesh Kumar, the arrest

options.A: is improper, since the officer must be satisfied that arrest is needed on the statutory grounds before making it
options.B: is improper only if the complainant is a relative of the husband and not the wife herself
options.C: is proper, since Sushil Kumar Sharma held that the offence cannot be questioned on grounds of misuse
options.D: is proper, because cruelty is a cognizable offence and arrest follows as of course once a complaint is lodged with the police

questions.explanation: Arrest is not automatic. The officer must record satisfaction that arrest is necessary under the statutory grounds, in line with the notice-of-appearance approach for lesser offences.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D equates cognizable with arrest as of course. Option B invents a distinction based on who is the complainant. Option C misreads Sushil Kumar Sharma, which upheld the provision but did not remove the safeguards on arrest.
questions.clat_trap: Two cases about the same provision pull in opposite directions, and a student merges them.
questions.language_trick: 'solely because' signals that the ground given is not enough.

questions.question: The decision in Sushil Kumar Sharma is best understood as holding that

options.A: the provision survives only because the Court read it down to apply to cases of death or grievous injury alone
options.B: courts may decline to apply a valid penal law in an individual case whenever the accused alleges misuse of it
options.C: misuse of section 498A makes it violate Article 14 unless a family welfare committee scrutinises every complaint first
options.D: a provision is not invalid merely because it may be misused in some cases

questions.explanation: The Court upheld the provision and treated misuse as a matter to be dealt with by the authorities and courts, not as a ground of invalidity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C adds a committee step that this decision did not impose. Option A invents a reading down. Option B gives courts a power to refuse to apply a valid law.
questions.clat_trap: Misuse is a popular theme, so a student leans to the answer that sounds sympathetic to the accused.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the passage.
I. The presumption of dowry death arises once the ingredients of dowry death are shown.
II. The 2005 Act prescribes imprisonment for cruelty committed by a husband.
III. Hiral Harsora struck down the words 'adult male' in the definition of respondent.
IV. Arnesh Kumar held that arrest for cruelty is automatic.
Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. The 2005 Act is a civil statute and Arnesh Kumar held that arrest is not automatic.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II confuses the civil Act with the penal provision on cruelty. Statement IV reverses Arnesh Kumar.
questions.clat_trap: A combination item rewards the student who checks each statement separately before choosing a pair.
questions.language_trick: 'only' in each option makes a single wrong statement fatal.

passages.title: Consent, Deceit and Sexual Offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
passages.passage: Section 63 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita defines rape and lists the circumstances in which sexual intercourse is rape. Consent is an unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, and the absence of physical resistance does not by itself imply consent. Intercourse with a woman under eighteen years of age is rape with or without her consent. An exception provides that intercourse by a man with his wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape. Section 64 prescribes imprisonment of not less than ten years which may extend to life. Section 69 creates a separate offence of sexual intercourse by deceitful means, which is not rape. It includes intercourse obtained by a false promise of marriage, a false promise of employment or promotion, inducement, or concealment of identity, and carries imprisonment up to ten years and fine. In Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v State of Maharashtra (2019), the Supreme Court held that consent given under a misconception of fact is vitiated only when the misconception is directly relevant to the act, and that a breach of a promise to marry must be distinguished from a promise made with no intention of keeping it. Earlier cases such as Uday v State of Karnataka (2003) and Dhruvaram Murlidhar Sonar v State of Maharashtra (2018) had drawn the same line. After the acquittal in Tukaram v State of Maharashtra (the Mathura case, 1979), Parliament amended the law in 1983 to deal with custodial rape and to create a presumption of absence of consent. In Independent Thought v Union of India (2017), the exception for wives was read down so as to apply only to wives not under eighteen years. In Lillu v State of Haryana (2013), the Court disapproved the two-finger test as violating privacy and dignity. The constitutional anchors are Articles 14, 15(3) and 21.

questions.question: A promises marriage to B and has consensual intercourse with her for two years. He later marries another woman under family pressure, and the court finds that he originally intended to marry B. On Pramod Suryabhan Pawar as described, A

options.A: is not guilty only if B was above eighteen years, since her age decides the character of the promise
options.B: is guilty of the offence of deceitful intercourse, since the promise was unkept and consent stands vitiated
options.C: is guilty of rape, since consent obtained on a promise of marriage is treated as no consent at all under the Sanhita in every case
options.D: has committed a breach of promise and not a false promise, and the consent was not vitiated by any deceit at the outset

questions.explanation: The promise was genuine when made. Its later breach is not a false promise, so there is no misconception of fact that vitiates consent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores that the promise was genuine when made. Option C turns a separate offence into rape. Option A brings in age, which has nothing to do with the nature of the promise.
questions.clat_trap: The facts end in a broken promise, which leads a student to equate breach with deceit.
questions.language_trick: 'breach' and 'false' are different words: one refers to later conduct and the other to the state of mind at the time of the promise.

questions.question: The decision in Tukaram v State of Maharashtra (the Mathura case) is remembered mainly because

options.A: it directed courts to stop questions on the sexual history of the survivor, which Lillu later endorsed
options.B: it struck down the exception for intercourse with a wife aged between fifteen and eighteen years as arbitrary
options.C: its acquittal led to the 1983 amendment on custodial rape and a presumption
options.D: it upheld the conviction of the policemen and directed a medical examination of the survivor in every case of alleged rape

questions.explanation: The public reaction to the acquittal led to the 1983 amendment, which created custodial rape and a presumption.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the outcome. Option B confuses Mathura with Independent Thought. Option A credits this case with an effect that came from other decisions.
questions.clat_trap: Landmark cases are mixed up with each other when the options use correct names for wrong holdings.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: After Independent Thought v Union of India, sexual intercourse by a man with his wife aged sixteen years is

options.A: rape only if the wife files a complaint within the limitation period for sexual offences
options.B: not rape, because the exception for sexual intercourse with a wife protects any wife above fifteen years of age, as it did earlier
options.C: an offence under the provision on deceitful means and not rape, as the marriage supplies her consent
options.D: rape, because the exception for wives was read down to apply only to wives not under eighteen years of age

questions.explanation: The Court read down the exception so that the age for a wife matches the age of eighteen for other women.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the position before the case. Option A adds a limitation condition not in the passage. Option C confuses the deceit offence with intercourse in marriage.
questions.clat_trap: The old age of fifteen sits in the first wrong option as a plausible number.
questions.language_trick: 'read down' means the exception remains but with a narrower field.

questions.question: The two-finger test on a survivor of rape was disapproved in Lillu v State of Haryana because

options.A: it can be used to prove consent but not to prove the fact of penetration by the accused
options.B: it violates her privacy and dignity
options.C: it was held to infringe Article 20(3) since the survivor is compelled to be a witness against herself
options.D: it is permitted only when the survivor consents in writing and a woman doctor is present at the examination

questions.explanation: The Court held that the test violates privacy and dignity of the survivor.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D converts the disapproval into a consent-based permission. Option A invents a limited use of the test. Option C misuses Article 20(3), which protects accused persons.
questions.clat_trap: Article 20(3) is a familiar article, so a student is attracted to it without checking whose right it is.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: A survivor who offers no physical resistance is to be taken as having consented to the act
options.B: Intercourse with a woman under eighteen is rape whether or not she agreed to it
options.C: Consent is an unequivocal voluntary agreement that may be communicated by gestures or any non-verbal form
options.D: A person who obtains intercourse by concealing his identity may be punished for deceitful intercourse

questions.explanation: The passage says that the absence of physical resistance does not by itself imply consent, so the statement in the correct option is the one that does not fit.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C, Option B and Option D each repeat the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem makes the student hunt for the false statement, and three true statements are written to look unusual.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT consistent' reverses the usual search.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Under the Sanhita, a woman's consent obtained by a false promise of marriage is treated as no consent, so such intercourse is rape.
Reason (R): Section 69 punishes sexual intercourse obtained by deceitful means, including a false promise of marriage, with imprisonment up to ten years and fine.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Section 69 creates a separate offence of deceitful intercourse that is not rape. Assertion is therefore false, while the Reason correctly states section 69.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is false because the false promise is treated under a distinct offence. R is true.
questions.clat_trap: R is a true statement that seems to support A, but it actually shows that the conduct is outside rape.
questions.language_trick: 'treated as no consent' and 'is rape' are the false parts of the assertion.

passages.title: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988: Demand, Acceptance, Sanction and Public Servants
passages.passage: The Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1964) led to the establishment of the Central Vigilance Commission and ultimately to the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, which was amended in 2018. Section 7 punishes a public servant who obtains or attempts to obtain undue advantage as a motive for performing public duty improperly. The 2018 amendment added section 8, which makes the giving of a bribe an offence, and section 9, which deals with commercial organisations. Section 13 on criminal misconduct was narrowed. Under section 19, a court cannot take cognizance of offences against a public servant without previous sanction of the competent authority. In Anil Kumar v M K Aiyappa (2013), the Court applied this requirement to cases brought on a private complaint. In Subramanian Swamy v Manmohan Singh (2012), the Court said that the competent authority should ordinarily decide a request for sanction within three months, extendable by one month where consultation with the law officer is needed. In P Satyanarayana Murthy v District Inspector of Police (2015), the Supreme Court held that proof of demand and acceptance of illegal gratification is essential and that mere recovery of money does not prove the offence. In Neeraj Dutta v State (NCT of Delhi) (2022), a Constitution Bench held that where the complainant dies or turns hostile, demand may be proved by other evidence, including circumstantial evidence, and the court may draw an inference from the proved facts. In CBI v Ramesh Gelli (2016), the Court held that officers of a private bank are public servants because they hold offices by virtue of which they perform a public duty in the business of banking, which is regulated in the public interest.

questions.question: A complainant who alleged a bribe demand dies before trial. No witness heard the demand directly, but the shadow witness and the recovery evidence are consistent with it. On Neeraj Dutta, the prosecution

options.A: may prove demand only through the earlier statement of the complainant recorded by the police at the pre-trap stage
options.B: must fail, because direct evidence of the complainant is indispensable
options.C: may prove demand by circumstantial evidence, and the court may infer demand and acceptance from proved facts
options.D: succeeds on recovery alone, because the presumption of illegal gratification arises without proof of any demand

questions.explanation: Neeraj Dutta allows other evidence, including circumstantial evidence, where direct evidence is unavailable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the rule that the Constitution Bench relaxed. Option A limits proof to a single class of evidence. Option D contradicts Satyanarayana Murthy.
questions.clat_trap: Two cases on demand pull in different directions, and a student applies the stricter rule to a situation where the Bench relaxed it.
questions.language_trick: 'may prove' is permissive and 'must fail' is absolute.

questions.question: A recovery of tainted currency from a public servant's table is proved, but there is no proof that he demanded or knowingly accepted it. On P Satyanarayana Murthy, the position is that

options.A: the accused must be acquitted only if the sanction for prosecution is also found to be invalid
options.B: recovery by itself raises the presumption of undue advantage against the public servant and the accused cannot rebut it
options.C: recovery proves acceptance, and so demand becomes unnecessary for the offence of obtaining undue advantage
options.D: mere recovery does not prove the offence, since demand and voluntary acceptance are essential ingredients of it

questions.explanation: The Court held that demand and acceptance are essential and that recovery alone is not enough.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B gives recovery the force of a presumption without proof of demand. Option C drops demand from the offence. Option A confuses sanction with proof of the ingredients.
questions.clat_trap: The recovery of money feels like a complete case, so the student skips the requirement of demand.
questions.language_trick: 'mere' signals that recovery is not enough.

questions.question: Officers of a private bank are 'public servants' under the 1988 Act because, per CBI v Ramesh Gelli,

options.A: private banks are instrumentalities of the State under Article 12 and so every officer holds a public office
options.B: the definition covers only officers of banks in which the Government holds a majority shareholding
options.C: the Act applies to every employee of a company that holds a licence from the State, whatever the nature of the functions
options.D: they hold offices by virtue of which they perform a public duty in banking, a business regulated in the public interest and the economy

questions.explanation: The test is the performance of a public duty by virtue of the office, and banking is such a duty when regulated in the public interest.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C turns a licence into a test. Option A imports the Article 12 test into the 1988 Act. Option B adds a shareholding condition.
questions.clat_trap: Article 12 and State ownership appear as natural tests but the Court's reasoning rested on public duty.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: On the time-limit for sanction under Subramanian Swamy v Manmohan Singh, the competent authority

options.A: must decide within fifteen days of receiving the request, with no extension whatever being allowed to it by any authority
options.B: should ordinarily decide within three months, extendable by one month for consulting the law officer
options.C: has no time-limit at all, since sanction is a discretion that courts cannot examine
options.D: should decide within one year, as the Act itself prescribes in the provision on sanction for prosecution

questions.explanation: The Court suggested a period of three months, extendable by a month where consultation is needed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a fifteen-day rule. Option C denies the time-limit. Option D attributes a one-year period to the Act.
questions.clat_trap: Numeric options tempt the student to guess from memory instead of the passage.
questions.language_trick: 'ordinarily' makes the time-limit a standard and not an absolute bar.

questions.question: A Magistrate is asked to take cognizance of a bribery offence alleged against a serving public servant on a private complaint, with no sanction. On section 19 and Aiyappa, the Magistrate

options.A: cannot take cognizance without sanction of the competent authority, even though the complaint is by a private person
options.B: may take cognizance if the complaint alleges that the public servant acted beyond the scope of duty
options.C: may take cognizance and call for sanction later, since sanction is a matter of evidence at the trial and not of cognizance
options.D: may take cognizance, since a private complaint falls outside the sanction requirement

questions.explanation: Section 19 bars cognizance without previous sanction, and Aiyappa applied the bar to private complaints.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D states the opposite of Aiyappa. Option C treats sanction as an evidentiary matter. Option B adds an exception the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: A private complainant is often thought to be outside State-controlled requirements, and the options use that instinct.
questions.language_trick: 'previous sanction' means sanction in advance of cognizance.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.
I. Section 8, added in 2018, makes the giving of a bribe an offence.
II. Neeraj Dutta permits proof of demand by circumstantial evidence in specified circumstances.
III. Mere recovery of tainted money suffices for conviction under section 7.
IV. The Santhanam Committee was constituted after the 1988 Act was passed.
Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I, III and IV only
options.D: I and II only

questions.explanation: Statements I and II restate the passage. Recovery alone is not enough, and the Committee of 1964 preceded the Act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement III contradicts Satyanarayana Murthy. Statement IV reverses the chronology.
questions.clat_trap: Chronology and the word 'mere' are the traps in this combination item.
questions.language_trick: 'mere' in statement III is the key word.

passages.title: Companies, Directors and Criminal Liability: BNS, NI Act and Jurisprudence on Corporate Personality
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita defines a person to include a company or association or body of persons, whether incorporated or not, so a company can be an accused. In Standard Chartered Bank v Directorate of Enforcement (2005), the Supreme Court held that a company can be prosecuted for offences for which imprisonment is mandatory, and that in such cases the court can impose a fine, since imprisonment cannot be imposed on a company. In Iridium India Telecom Ltd v Motorola Inc (2011), the Court held that a company can be liable for offences requiring mens rea, because the mind of the person who is the directing mind of the company is attributed to it when he acts for it. In Aneeta Hada v Godfather Travels and Tours (2012), the Court held that, in a prosecution under section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the liability of a director is vicarious and arises only where the company, as the principal offender, is also arraigned. In Maksud Saiyed v State of Gujarat (2008), the Court held that directors cannot be made liable merely because of their office without specific allegations. In Sunil Bharti Mittal v CBI (2015), the Court held that the person who is only a head of a company can be made liable for its offence only if he is shown to be the alter ego of the company or a statute specifically makes him liable. The Sanhita also deals with organised crime by syndicates in section 111. Jurisprudence offers several explanations of corporate personality. The concession or fiction theory associated with Savigny says that a company is a legal person because the State recognises it as one. The realist theory associated with Gierke says that a company has a real will and personality of its own. The bracket or symbolist theory sees a company as a name for the rights and duties of its members. The decision in Salomon v Salomon (1897) established that a company is distinct from its members.

questions.question: A company is charged with an offence for which the law prescribes imprisonment as a mandatory punishment along with fine. On Standard Chartered Bank, the prosecution

options.A: must fail, because a company cannot be sentenced to imprisonment and so cannot be prosecuted at all for such an offence under the law
options.B: may proceed against the company only if the statute itself names the company as an accused
options.C: may proceed against the company and the court may impose the fine alone, since imprisonment cannot be imposed on a company
options.D: may proceed only against the directors, since a company as a legal fiction cannot be prosecuted

questions.explanation: The Court held that a company may be prosecuted and the court may impose a fine where imprisonment cannot be applied.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A converts an inability to impose one punishment into an immunity. Option D denies that a company can be prosecuted. Option B adds a requirement that the statute name the company.
questions.clat_trap: The impossibility of imprisoning a company leads a student to infer that the company cannot be prosecuted.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The reasoning in Iridium India Telecom v Motorola for holding a company liable for offences needing mens rea is that

options.A: a company can be convicted only for strict liability offences, as mens rea cannot be attributed to it
options.B: the mind of the directing person is attributed to the company when he acts for it in the course of its business
options.C: a company has a mind of its own as the realist theory insists, which is distinct from that of every person acting for it
options.D: the collective intention of the shareholders is imputed to it whenever any employee commits the act

questions.explanation: The Court attributed the state of mind of the directing mind to the company when he acts for it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C gives the company its own mind, which is not the reasoning used. Option D imputes the shareholders' intention. Option A contradicts the holding.
questions.clat_trap: The names of theories in the passage are used as decoys in the wrong options.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A complaint against a company names its chairman only because he heads the group, with no act alleged against him. On Sunil Bharti Mittal v CBI, the chairman

options.A: cannot be made vicariously liable merely by his office, unless he is the alter ego of the company or a statute makes him liable
options.B: is not liable, because directors can never be liable for the offences of a company under any statute
options.C: is liable if the company is convicted, since a company acts only through its principal officer
options.D: is liable, since the person at the head of a company is always taken to be its directing mind

questions.explanation: A mere head is not liable unless he is the alter ego or the statute provides for it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D and Option C equate office with guilt. Option B uses 'never' and ignores the statutory exceptions.
questions.clat_trap: A senior office in the group makes liability look natural and the exceptions are the last part of the correct option.
questions.language_trick: 'merely by his office' is the key limiting phrase.

questions.question: A complaint under section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is filed against a director alone, and the company is not arraigned. On Aneeta Hada, the complaint is

options.A: maintainable, since directors are liable as persons in charge whether or not the company is made an accused
options.B: not maintainable, because the liability of the director is vicarious and arises only when the company, as principal offender, is also arraigned
options.C: not maintainable only if the director had resigned before the cheque was dishonoured
options.D: maintainable, because the company is only a nominal party whose absence can be cured by an amendment at trial

questions.explanation: Vicarious liability presupposes the principal's liability and so the company must be arraigned.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A separates the director from the company. Option D treats the company as a nominal party. Option C confuses the point with a defence of resignation.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'vicarious' carries the answer, but students rush to the option about the person in charge.
questions.language_trick: 'only when' in the correct option states a condition.

questions.question: The concession theory of corporate personality holds that

options.A: a company has a real personality of its own, independent of any recognition by the State
options.B: a company is a trust in which the members' property is held by managers
options.C: a company is a legal person only because the State recognises it as one under law
