options.D: the personality of a company is a mere name for the rights and duties of its members taken together as a body

questions.explanation: The concession or fiction theory ties personality to State recognition, associated with Savigny in the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the realist theory. Option D states the bracket theory. Option B describes a trust and is not a theory of personality in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Three theories are named in the passage, and the options exchange them.
questions.language_trick: 'concession' and 'recognition' are synonyms in this context.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A director cannot be convicted of an offence under the Sanhita merely because he is a director of the company that committed it.
Reason (R): The Sanhita's definition of person includes a company, so the company alone is the offender and its directors can never be liable.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Assertion is correct, as Maksud Saiyed and Sunil Bharti Mittal show. The Reason is false, because directors may be liable on proof of their own acts, alter ego status or statutory provisions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R overstates with 'alone' and 'never'. A is supported by the cases in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A true assertion is paired with a reason that sounds like a legal explanation but contradicts the cases.
questions.language_trick: 'merely' in A and 'never' in R decide the two halves.

passages.title: Common Intention, Common Object, Abetment and Conspiracy in the BNS
passages.passage: Section 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita provides that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of them is liable for that act as if it were done by him alone. Section 189 deals with unlawful assembly of five or more persons, and section 190 makes every member of such an assembly guilty of an offence committed in prosecution of the common object. In Barendra Kumar Ghosh v King-Emperor (1925), the Privy Council held that a person who merely stood and waited may be a participant in the criminal act, since 'they also serve who only stand and wait'. In Mahbub Shah v King-Emperor (1945), it was held that common intention requires a prearranged plan and participation of the accused in the act. In Pandurang v State of Hyderabad (1955), the Supreme Court held that the intention may be formed on the spot, but there must be a meeting of minds. In Ramaswamy Ayyangar v State of Tamil Nadu (1976), the Court held that the provision on common intention does not create a substantive offence and lays down a rule of joint liability. Abetment under section 45 may be by instigation, conspiracy or intentional aid. Under section 61, an agreement to commit an offence is itself a criminal conspiracy, and an agreement to do an illegal act that is not an offence requires an act besides the agreement. In Kehar Singh v State (1988), the Court held that conspiracy rests on an agreement. Section 62 deals with attempt, and in Abhayanand Mishra v State of Bihar (1961), the Court held that the submission of a false application to a university, claiming to be a graduate in order to sit an examination, was an attempt to cheat, and that mere preparation differs from an attempt.

questions.question: Four persons plan to rob a house. A and B enter, and C stands guard at the gate in furtherance of the plan, while D, a stranger, joins C with no knowledge of it. A kills the owner in the course of the robbery. Under section 3(5) and Barendra Kumar Ghosh, C

options.A: is liable as a participant, since standing guard in furtherance of the plan counts as participation
options.B: is liable only for abetment, since he did no act of violence himself and so cannot share liability for the act
options.C: is liable only if D also shares the plan, since the common intention must be that of all those present at the place
options.D: is not liable for the act, because only those who physically enter the house and commit the act are participants

questions.explanation: A person who stands by to assist in a prearranged plan is a participant, as Barendra Kumar Ghosh holds.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reads participation as physical performance. Option B downgrades the standing guard to an abettor. Option C makes the intention of a stranger decisive.
questions.clat_trap: The standing guard did no violent act, which leads a student to conclude that he has no liability.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The difference between common intention under section 3(5) and common object under section 190 is that

options.A: common intention applies to any number of persons, but common object applies only to groups of more than ten persons
options.B: common object requires proof of a prearranged plan, whereas common intention may arise without any prior concert
options.C: common intention creates a substantive offence of its own, whereas common object only declares a rule of liability
options.D: common intention needs a prearranged plan or a meeting of minds, whereas common object attaches to members of an assembly of five or more persons

questions.explanation: Common intention involves a shared plan, while common object is an attribute of the unlawful assembly of five or more.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C reverses the Ramaswamy Ayyangar point. Option B swaps the two concepts. Option A invents a numerical threshold of more than ten.
questions.clat_trap: The two provisions are often treated as equivalents and the options swap their features.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The effect of the provision on common intention, as stated in Ramaswamy Ayyangar, is that it

options.A: creates a separate offence of joint action punishable independently of the offence committed by the participants
options.B: applies only if every participant has committed an overt act contributing to the offence charged against all of them
options.C: makes each member liable only for the part he physically performed in the commission of the offence
options.D: does not create a substantive offence but lays down a rule of joint liability

questions.explanation: The Court held that it is a rule of evidence and joint liability, not a substantive offence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states what the Court rejected. Option B adds an overt-act requirement that Barendra Kumar Ghosh rejects. Option C contradicts the idea of 'as if done by him alone'.
questions.clat_trap: 'joint liability' sounds like a separate offence, which the first wrong option exploits.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Three persons agree to commit an offence, but none does any act beyond the agreement. On section 61 as described, they are

options.A: guilty of abetment by instigation, which needs no act by the abettors beyond the agreement
options.B: not guilty of anything, because conspiracy needs an overt act beyond the agreement in every case without exception whatever
options.C: guilty of criminal conspiracy, since the agreement to commit an offence is itself the gist of the conspiracy
options.D: guilty only of attempt, because the agreement puts the offence in the course of being committed

questions.explanation: An agreement to commit an offence is itself a criminal conspiracy, while an overt act is needed only for an agreement to do an illegal act that is not an offence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B overstates the act requirement. Option D confuses agreement with attempt. Option A wrongly describes the nature of the abetment.
questions.clat_trap: The need for an act beyond the agreement applies only to one type of conspiracy and not to the other.
questions.language_trick: 'in every case' is an overstatement.

questions.question: A person submits to a university a false application claiming to be a graduate so that he can sit an examination, and is caught afterwards. On Abhayanand Mishra, the application

options.A: is no offence, since the intention to cheat is not punishable until a person has actually been deceived
options.B: is mere preparation, because an attempt begins only when the university acts upon the application
options.C: can amount to an attempt to cheat, since submitting it was the last step he needed to take towards his purpose
options.D: is abetment, since the applicant instigated the university to confer the degree on him

questions.explanation: The Court held that the false application was an attempt and not mere preparation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B places the start of the attempt too late. Option A requires actual deception. Option D confuses the applicant's act with abetment of another.
questions.clat_trap: Preparation and attempt are close in time, and a student treats the lack of result as the absence of an offence.
questions.language_trick: 'last step' captures the test of proximity.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.
I. The provision on common intention does not create a substantive offence.
II. Common intention under Barendra Kumar Ghosh requires physical participation in the act itself.
III. A member of an unlawful assembly may be liable for an offence committed in prosecution of the common object.
IV. An agreement to commit an offence is itself a criminal conspiracy.
Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, III and IV only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, III and IV state the passage. Statement II is wrong because a person standing by may be a participant.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II reverses Barendra Kumar Ghosh.
questions.clat_trap: Statement II is the only one that departs from the passage, so it must be spotted among three true statements.
questions.language_trick: 'physical' is the only word that makes statement II false.

passages.title: Fair Trial, Legal Aid and the New Procedural Code: Articles 21, 22(1) and 39A
passages.passage: Article 21 forbids deprivation of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law, and since Maneka Gandhi that procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. A fair trial is therefore part of Article 21. Article 22(1) adds that an arrested person shall not be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice. Article 39A, inserted by the Forty-second Amendment in 1976, directs the State to ensure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which followed the work of committees led by Justice Krishna Iyer and Justice Bhagwati, created the National Legal Services Authority and Lok Adalats. In Hussainara Khatoon (1979) the Supreme Court held that free legal aid is an ingredient of reasonable, fair and just procedure and that speedy trial is implicit in Article 21. In M. H. Hoskot (1978) the Court extended legal aid to a convicted person who wished to appeal. Khatri v State of Bihar (1981) held that the Magistrate must inform the accused of the right to free legal aid, and that the State cannot plead financial or administrative inability to provide it. In Suk Das v Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh (1986) the Court held that the right does not depend on a request by the accused, and that a trial in which legal aid was not offered is vitiated unless the accused refused it. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita now permits statements, inquiries and trials to be conducted through audio-video electronic means and allows summons to be served electronically. It also provides for trial in the absence of a proclaimed offender, after charges are framed and a prescribed period has passed. Critics say that this last provision must be read with Article 21, because a trial is fair only if the accused has had a real opportunity to be heard.

questions.question: Under Khatri v State of Bihar, a Magistrate who produces an unrepresented accused and says nothing about legal aid has

options.A: failed in a duty cast on the court, since the right to free legal aid exists whether or not the accused asks for it and cannot be defeated by the State's plea of financial limits
options.B: failed in a duty that arises only after conviction, when the appeal stage gives rise to the right to a lawyer at the State's expense
options.C: committed a lapse only if the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment, which alone attract legal aid at the State's cost
options.D: committed no lapse, because legal aid is available only on a request made by the accused or by a relative before the Magistrate

questions.explanation: Khatri places the duty to inform on the Magistrate, and the State cannot plead inability. The right does not wait for a request.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D makes the right depend on a request, which Khatri and Suk Das reject. Option C limits the right to the gravest offences without support in the passage. Option B moves the right to the appeal stage, which was Hoskot's separate extension.
questions.clat_trap: Three options narrow the right by a condition (request, gravity, stage). The correct one is the only option that states the duty as unconditional.
questions.language_trick: 'whether or not the accused asks' signals the unconditional duty.

questions.question: A poor labourer is convicted after a trial in which he had no lawyer and was never told of legal aid. Applying Suk Das, the conviction

options.A: stands, since Article 39A is a Directive Principle and cannot be used to set aside a verdict of a competent court
options.B: is vitiated only if he had applied in writing for State legal assistance before the trial began and was refused
options.C: stands, because a lawyer is a right only of persons in custody under Article 22(1), and not of a person facing trial
options.D: is vitiated for want of legal aid at the trial, and he need not have asked for it, unless he had refused it when offered

questions.explanation: Suk Das makes the denial of legal aid at trial fatal, and the right is independent of a request. The only escape is a refusal by the accused.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C confines Article 22(1) to custody, ignoring Article 21. Option A treats Article 39A as the only source, while Hussainara reads legal aid into Article 21. Option B reintroduces the request requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options use real constitutional provisions to reach a wrong conclusion, so recognition of the provision is not enough.
questions.language_trick: 'unless he had refused it' is the proviso that completes the rule.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly traces the constitutional source of the right to free legal aid as the passage presents it?

options.A: Article 22(1) alone, since it is the only provision that mentions a legal practitioner and so limits the right to arrested persons
options.B: Article 21 read with Articles 39A and 22(1), the aid being part of reasonable, fair and just procedure
options.C: Article 39A alone, which, though a Directive Principle, became enforceable against courts through the Forty-second Amendment
options.D: Article 14 alone, because unequal access to a lawyer violates equal protection of the laws

questions.explanation: The Court read Article 39A and Article 22(1) into the fair-procedure guarantee of Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option C each pick one provision as the sole source. Option D relies on Article 14 only.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'alone' appears in all three wrong options. The right is a composite one.
questions.language_trick: 'read with' marks a combined source.

questions.question: The Hoskot decision is best described as extending legal aid to

options.A: a convicted person who is pursuing an appeal against conviction and sentence
options.B: persons sentenced to death alone, since only a capital sentence engages Article 21 at appeal
options.C: only persons arrested for offences triable by a Court of Session, up to the stage of framing of charge
options.D: undertrial prisoners held beyond half of the maximum sentence, as sole beneficiaries

questions.explanation: Hoskot carried legal aid forward from trial to appeal after conviction.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C confines the right to a trial stage and a class of offences. Option B limits it to capital cases. Option D invents a detention threshold.
questions.clat_trap: Detailed distractors make the short, simple answer look incomplete. A short option can be the right one.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The provision on trial in the absence of a proclaimed offender raises an Article 21 concern mainly because

options.A: the provision abolishes the need for a proclamation, so any absconding suspect can be tried at once without any prior process
options.B: it allows conviction on the statement of the investigating officer alone, in place of evidence led before the court
options.C: a person may be adjudged guilty without taking part, though charges must be framed and a period must elapse first
options.D: it bars the convict from appealing against the sentence passed in his absence

questions.explanation: The concern is the absence of a hearing, tempered by the preconditions the passage lists.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the passage, which keeps the proclamation. Option B invents a rule of proof. Option D invents a bar on appeal.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option includes the safeguards, which makes it look weaker than the alarming wrong options.
questions.language_trick: 'though' balances the concern with the safeguards.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Article 39A, being a Directive Principle, is by itself a fundamental right to free legal aid enforceable against the State. Reason (R): Article 39A was inserted into the Constitution by the Forty-second Amendment in 1976.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Article 39A is a Directive Principle that the Court has enforced through Article 21 and 22(1). R is true as stated in the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is false because the right is enforceable through Article 21, not Article 39A alone. R is true but does not make A true.
questions.clat_trap: A true R beside a false A tempts students to link them.
questions.language_trick: 'by itself' makes A false.

passages.title: Territorial and Extra-territorial Reach of Indian Criminal Law
passages.passage: Article 245(2) provides that no law made by Parliament shall be deemed invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation. Article 20(1) separately protects an accused from retrospective penal laws. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita applies to offences committed within India, to offences committed by Indian citizens anywhere, and to offences committed by any person on a ship or aircraft registered in India, wherever it may be. It also contains a provision, new in form, on the abetment in India of an offence committed outside India. Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, an offence committed outside India is inquired into or tried as if it had been committed at any place where the accused may be found, but the Central Government's previous sanction is needed. In Mobarik Ali Ahmed v State of Bombay (1957), a foreign national outside India who cheated an Indian by correspondence was held triable in India because the effect of his act was felt in India. In GVK Industries v Income Tax Officer (2011), the Court held that Parliament may legislate with extra-territorial effect but only where there is a sufficient nexus between the law and India, and that Article 245(2) bars a challenge based only on the law's operation outside India. The older Lotus principle of the Permanent Court of International Justice allows a State to extend its jurisdiction unless a rule of international law forbids it. The Extradition Act, 1962 governs the surrender of fugitives. In Abu Salem v State of Maharashtra (2010), where Portugal had extradited the appellant on assurances about the maximum penalty, the Court held that the Government of India must honour its assurance, while stating that the courts are not themselves bound by an executive assurance in applying the Code. The principle of specialty prevents a surrendered person from being tried for offences other than those for which surrender was granted, unless the surrendering State agrees.

questions.question: A foreign national, while abroad, deceives an Indian by letters and emails and obtains property in India. Under Mobarik Ali Ahmed, Indian courts

options.A: have no jurisdiction because the accused was never physically present in India when the acts took place
options.B: may try him, as the effect arose in India
options.C: may try him only if he has first been extradited from the country of residence under a treaty in force
options.D: may try him only after the Government of India has obtained the consent of his State of nationality

questions.explanation: Mobarik Ali Ahmed accepted the effects doctrine: the act was felt in India, so Indian courts could try it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A requires physical presence. Option C makes extradition a precondition to jurisdiction, but it is a means of securing the person. Option D invents a consent of the State of nationality.
questions.clat_trap: A short, plain option is the right one; the longer options add formal-sounding conditions.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: On the passage, Article 245(2) of the Constitution means that

options.A: criminal laws cannot operate outside India, and only civil and tax laws can do so
options.B: an Act of Parliament is not void merely for operating beyond India, though a nexus with India is still required
options.C: a law operating abroad is valid only where the foreign State has consented to its application by treaty
options.D: Parliament may legislate on any matter anywhere in the world with no need for any link to India or its citizens at all

questions.explanation: Article 245(2) removes the objection of extra-territoriality, while GVK Industries keeps the nexus requirement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D drops the nexus. Option C adds a consent condition. Option A wrongly separates criminal laws from others.
questions.clat_trap: 'any', 'at all' and 'cannot' make the wrong options sound absolute, but the correct option is a two-part rule.
questions.language_trick: 'merely' limits the point of Article 245(2).

questions.question: An Indian citizen commits an offence on foreign soil. Under the position described in the passage

options.A: the citizen is liable under the Sanhita, but trial in India needs the Central Government's prior sanction
options.B: the citizen is liable only if the foreign country has asked for his surrender
options.C: the citizen is liable, and any Magistrate in India may try the offence directly with no further permission of any kind
options.D: the citizen is not liable under the Sanhita because criminal law operates only within the territory of India and its coastal waters

questions.explanation: The Sanhita applies to citizens anywhere, and the procedural Code requires sanction for trial of an offence committed outside India.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D denies extra-territorial reach over citizens. Option C omits the sanction. Option B turns on a request for surrender.
questions.clat_trap: Two parts (liability and sanction) must both be right.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: In Abu Salem (2010), the Court's treatment of the assurances given to Portugal shows that

options.A: the executive must honour the limits it promised to the surrendering State, but the courts remain free to apply the Code to the offences tried before them
options.B: the assurances are legally unenforceable and the Government may disregard them once the fugitive is in India
options.C: the courts are bound to read the promised limit into the statute and may not impose any sentence beyond it
options.D: the surrender made every offence in the charge-sheet triable, including those not covered by the extradition request

questions.explanation: The assurance binds the Government, not the courts. It does not extend trial to unsurrendered offences, because specialty applies.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C binds the courts. Option B reduces the assurance to nothing. Option D ignores specialty.
questions.clat_trap: The passage states a split between executive and judicial obligation, which a hurried reader flattens.
questions.language_trick: 'but' joins two separate obligations.

questions.question: A law of Parliament seeks to tax income earned wholly abroad by a foreign company from dealings with no link to India. Following GVK Industries, the law is

options.A: valid, since foreign companies have no fundamental rights and so no standing to question Parliament's competence
options.B: valid, because Article 245(2) bars any challenge based on extra-territorial operation, whether or not a nexus exists
options.C: open to challenge, since extra-territorial reach needs a real nexus with India, whatever Article 245(2) says
options.D: void, because Parliament cannot legislate for foreign companies at all

questions.explanation: Article 245(2) stops the extra-territoriality objection but the Court requires a nexus, so the challenge on lack of nexus is open.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reads Article 245(2) as absolute. Option A mixes standing with legislative competence. Option D denies power altogether.
questions.clat_trap: Article 245(2) seems to settle the matter but the nexus requirement survives.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the passage. I. Article 245(2) validates an Act of Parliament operating outside India, but a nexus with India is still required. II. Under the Mobarik Ali Ahmed principle, a person who was abroad when he acted cannot be tried in India even if the effect arose in India. III. Under the principle of specialty, a surrendered person may be tried only for the offences for which surrender was granted unless the surrendering State agrees. IV. An offence committed abroad by a citizen can be tried in India without any sanction.

options.A: I only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. Statement II reverses Mobarik Ali Ahmed. Statement IV ignores the requirement of sanction.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option I only omits III. Option II and IV only selects both false statements. Option I, III and IV only adds the false IV.
questions.clat_trap: A combination that omits a true statement tempts the student who is cautious about III.
questions.language_trick: 'unless the surrendering State agrees' is the qualification in III.

passages.title: Prisoners' Rights, Remission and Clemency: Articles 14, 21, 72 and 161
passages.passage: A person does not lose the protection of Article 21 on entering prison. In Sunil Batra v Delhi Administration (1978) the Supreme Court held that imprisonment does not end a prisoner's fundamental rights, and subjected solitary confinement and the use of fetters to judicial scrutiny. In Sheela Barse v State of Maharashtra (1983) the Court gave directions for the safety of women in custody. The Prisons Act, 1894 and the Model Prison Manual govern conditions, and a Model Prisons Act of 2023 has been circulated to the States (verify current status). In Sukanya Shantha v Union of India (October 2024) the Court struck down provisions of several State prison manuals that allotted work and barracks by caste and treated certain communities as habitual offenders, holding that they violated Articles 14, 15, 17 and 21. On release, the sentence may be reduced by remission. Articles 72 and 161 give the President and the Governors a constitutional power of pardon and commutation, while the procedural Code gives the appropriate Government a statutory power of remission. In Union of India v V. Sriharan (2015), a Constitution Bench held that a court may sentence a convict to imprisonment for the remainder of his life, or to a fixed term beyond fourteen years, without the Executive being able to cut it short by ordinary remission, while the constitutional clemency powers remain untouched. In Epuru Sudhakar v Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006) the Court held that orders under Article 161 are open to judicial review on limited grounds such as mala fides, irrelevant considerations and arbitrariness. In Bilkis Yakub Rasool v Union of India (January 2024) the Court quashed the premature release of eleven convicts, holding that the State where the trial took place, and not the State in which they were imprisoned, was the appropriate Government, and that an earlier order allowing the other State to decide had been obtained by suppressing facts.

questions.question: Following Sunil Batra, imprisonment

options.A: permits solitary confinement as a routine measure whenever the jail superintendent thinks it necessary
options.B: leaves rights intact only for undertrials and not for convicts serving a sentence of imprisonment
options.C: suspends fundamental rights until release, except the right to approach the High Court for a writ of habeas corpus
options.D: does not end a prisoner's right under Article 21

questions.explanation: Sunil Batra held that prison walls do not shut out Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C suspends rights. Option B limits protection to undertrials. Option A treats solitary confinement as routine.
questions.clat_trap: The short correct option is overshadowed by long wrong options that mention familiar remedies.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Sukanya Shantha decision of 2024 struck down jail manual provisions that

options.A: allotted cleaning and cooking duties by caste and segregated prisoners by caste, offending Articles 14, 15, 17 and 21
options.B: denied parole to prisoners convicted of offences against women, on the view that Article 14 forbids any classification of convicts
options.C: prescribed rigorous imprisonment for all prisoners irrespective of the sentence imposed, contrary to the reformative aim of Article 21
options.D: allowed visits by lawyers only during a limited period in the week

questions.explanation: The decision dealt with caste-based division of labour and segregation and with the 'habitual offender' references to communities.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C and Option B describe provisions that the passage does not mention. Option D is a procedural complaint unrelated to caste.
questions.clat_trap: A familiar theme (reformative punishment) is used as a decoy for a caste-specific holding.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Under Union of India v V. Sriharan (2015), a court sentencing a person to imprisonment for life may

options.A: impose a fixed term only when the offence is one of terrorism or sedition
options.B: order a fixed term well beyond fourteen years or the whole of his life, leaving the constitutional clemency powers untouched
options.C: name the sentence and do nothing more, as the appropriate Government alone decides the minimum actual period to serve
options.D: order a term of life that automatically ends after fourteen years of actual custody, whatever the gravity of the offence or the reasons recorded by the sentencing court

questions.explanation: The Constitution Bench allowed fixed-term and whole-life sentences, beyond the reach of ordinary remission, while Articles 72 and 161 remain.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D states a rule of automatic release that the Bench rejected. Option C leaves the whole question to the Government. Option A invents a category restriction.
questions.clat_trap: The 'fourteen years' figure is a familiar number used in the wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'beyond fourteen' is where the Bench departed from the older understanding.

questions.question: In Bilkis Yakub Rasool (January 2024), the Court quashed the remission orders mainly because

options.A: the Constitution gives only the President and not the Governor the power to grant remission
options.B: the State that granted remission was not the appropriate Government, which is the State where the trial took place, and the earlier order permitting it had been obtained by suppressing facts
options.C: remission can never be granted to persons convicted of rape or murder, whatever the Government and the circumstances
options.D: the convicts had not completed fourteen years of imprisonment, which alone makes remission impermissible

questions.explanation: The Court held that the State of the trial was the appropriate Government and that the earlier order was a product of suppression of facts.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C states an absolute bar that does not exist. Option D invents a threshold. Option A confuses clemency with remission under the Code.
questions.clat_trap: The option combines two grounds; both are required to match the decision.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Epuru Sudhakar supports the view that an order under Article 161 is

options.A: open to limited judicial review
options.B: reviewable only by the President, who alone may correct an order passed by a Governor
options.C: reviewable on the merits as an ordinary appeal from the Government's decision on the facts
options.D: wholly immune from review as it is an exercise of sovereign prerogative power by the Governor

questions.explanation: The Court reviews such orders only on narrow grounds such as mala fides and arbitrariness.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D claims complete immunity. Option C converts review into appeal. Option B invents a role for the President.
questions.clat_trap: Complete immunity and full appeal are the two extremes; the correct answer lies between.
questions.language_trick: 'limited' is the key word.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The State in which the trial of the offender took place is the appropriate Government to decide a remission application. Reason (R): The appropriate Government for remission is always the State in which the convict is lodged in prison.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A reflects Bilkis Yakub Rasool. R reverses the rule and uses 'always'.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is false because the place of imprisonment does not fix the appropriate Government.
questions.clat_trap: R reverses the rule using the same words.
questions.language_trick: 'always' makes R false.

passages.title: The NDPS Act: Twin Conditions, Safeguards on Search and Statements
passages.passage: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 gives effect to Article 47 of the Constitution, which directs the State to endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption of intoxicating drugs injurious to health, except for medicinal purposes. Section 37 provides that a person accused of certain offences, including offences involving commercial quantity, shall not be released on bail unless the Public Prosecutor has had an opportunity to oppose and the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. These are the twin conditions. Section 50 gives a person about to be searched the right to be taken before a gazetted officer or a Magistrate. In State of Punjab v Baldev Singh (1999) the Constitution Bench held that the suspect must be informed of this right. In Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja v State of Gujarat (2010) the Court held that the duty to inform is mandatory and that substantial compliance is not enough. In Toofan Singh v State of Tamil Nadu (2020) a Bench of three judges held that officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau, who investigate under the Act, are police officers for the purposes of the Evidence Act, so that statements made to them during investigation cannot be used as confessions to convict the maker. In Mohan Lal v State of Punjab (2018) the Court held that fair investigation is part of fair trial, and that the informant and the investigating officer should not be the same person. Mandatory minimum sentences under the Act are tested against Articles 14 and 21 in the light of Mithu v State of Punjab (1983), where a mandatory death sentence was struck down. The passage does not suggest that Article 47 creates a fundamental right.

questions.question: At the bail stage in a case involving commercial quantity of contraband, the court must

options.A: give the prosecutor a chance to oppose and be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and will not offend while on bail
options.B: grant bail as of right because the accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty, the twin conditions applying only after a conviction and not at the bail stage
options.C: refuse bail in every case, since commercial quantity bars bail under any circumstance whatever
options.D: grant bail on the strength of the accused's age alone, since the twin conditions are directory in character

questions.explanation: Section 37 sets twin conditions, and the court must be satisfied on both, after hearing the prosecutor.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B says the conditions apply only after conviction. Option D treats them as directory. Option C says bail is always barred.
questions.clat_trap: Two options move to opposite extremes (always or never), while the correct option is conditional.
questions.language_trick: 'reasonable grounds for believing' is a standard of satisfaction, not of proof.

questions.question: A search of the person under section 50 is conducted without telling the suspect of his right to be taken before a gazetted officer or Magistrate. The recovery is

options.A: vitiated only if the recovery was from the suspect's residence
options.B: vitiated for non-compliance, since the right to be informed is mandatory and substantial compliance does not cure the omission
options.C: valid if the officer who made the search holds a rank above that of an Inspector
options.D: valid, since the right to be searched before a gazetted officer is only a courtesy that the suspect must himself demand at the time of the search

questions.explanation: Baldev Singh and Jadeja require the suspect to be informed; omission is fatal, and substantial compliance does not suffice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D makes the right depend on a demand. Option C brings in rank, which does not cure the omission. Option A limits the rule to a residence, though the passage speaks of the person.
questions.clat_trap: 'substantial compliance' is a doctrine that tempts a reader to save the recovery.
questions.language_trick: 'mandatory' and 'not enough' are the decisive words.

questions.question: Toofan Singh v State of Tamil Nadu (2020) holds that a statement made to an officer of the Narcotics Control Bureau during investigation

options.A: can be relied on as a confession, since a narcotics officer is not a police officer, being appointed under a special statute
options.B: is admissible only against co-accused and never against the person who made the statement
options.C: cannot be relied on as a confession to convict the maker, because those officers are police officers for the purposes of the Evidence Act provision
options.D: is admissible only if it is recorded before a gazetted officer, whose presence cures its defect as evidence

questions.explanation: Toofan Singh treated those officers as police officers, so statements to them cannot be used as confessions against the maker.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the holding. Option D supplies a cure that the decision does not mention. Option B invents a rule restricted to co-accused.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is longest and detailed; the distractors apply real evidence doctrines to the wrong effect.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The decision in Mohan Lal v State of Punjab (2018) is best summarised as holding that

options.A: recovery from a public place requires prior sanction of a Magistrate
options.B: the informant and the investigator should not be the same person, since a fair investigation is part of a fair trial
options.C: an informant who also investigates is permitted so long as the accused has been given the benefit of the twin conditions for bail
options.D: a prosecution under the Act fails whenever the investigating officer is of a rank below that of Superintendent of Police

questions.explanation: Mohan Lal links an independent investigation to the fair trial guarantee.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C confuses bail with investigation. Option D invents a rank threshold. Option A invents a sanction requirement.
questions.clat_trap: 'twin conditions' is a familiar phrase used to mislead.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Article 47 of the Constitution is relevant to the NDPS scheme because

options.A: it empowers the Union alone to regulate narcotic substances to the exclusion of State laws
options.B: it directs the State to endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption of intoxicating drugs injurious to health, supporting the Act's purpose without creating a fundamental right
options.C: it exempts offences under the Act from the guarantees in Articles 20 to 22
options.D: it confers a fundamental right to be free of drugs that may be enforced against private persons

questions.explanation: Article 47 is a Directive Principle that supports the Act. The passage states that it creates no fundamental right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D turns the Directive Principle into a fundamental right. Option A invents an exclusion of State law. Option C invents an exemption from Articles 20 to 22.
questions.clat_trap: A longer, more careful option expresses the Directive Principle accurately.
questions.language_trick: 'endeavour' signals a non-enforceable duty.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the passage. I. The twin conditions for bail apply to offences involving commercial quantity under the Act. II. Substantial compliance with the section on search of the person is enough according to Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja. III. Toofan Singh holds that officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau are not police officers for the Evidence Act. IV. Article 47 is a Directive Principle.

options.A: I only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: I and IV only
options.D: II and III only

questions.explanation: Statements I and IV are correct. Statement II is the opposite of Jadeja and statement III is the opposite of Toofan Singh.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option I only omits IV. Option I and III only includes the false III. Option II and III only is the pair of false statements.
questions.clat_trap: Two statements are inversions of holdings; both are stated in the exact language of the passage.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law, Privacy and Free Speech
passages.title: Defamation, Reputation and Free Speech: Articles 19(1)(a), 19(2) and 21
passages.passage: Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita defines defamation and punishes it with simple imprisonment for up to two years, or fine, or both, or community service. The offence has exceptions, including imputation of truth made for the public good, good-faith opinion on the conduct of a public servant, and fair comment on public questions. Under the procedural Code, the Magistrate takes cognizance on a complaint by the person aggrieved. Article 19(2) lists defamation as a ground on which the State may impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech. In Subramanian Swamy v Union of India (2016), the Supreme Court upheld the criminal provisions on defamation, holding that reputation is part of the right to life and dignity under Article 21, and that criminal defamation is a reasonable restriction within Article 19(2). The Court rejected the argument that a purely civil remedy would suffice. In Kiran Bedi v Committee of Inquiry (1989) the Court had described reputation as an inseparable aspect of human dignity. In R. Rajagopal v State of Tamil Nadu (1994) the Court held that the press may publish matters of public record, including court records, without liability for violation of privacy, and that a public official cannot claim damages for defamation unless the publication was made with reckless disregard for the truth. In Khushboo v Kanniammal (2010) the Court held that the expression of views, even unpopular ones, does not amount to defamation merely because some find them offensive. Theorists have framed the tension differently. John Stuart Mill's harm principle justifies State restriction of speech only to prevent harm to others, while Justice Holmes spoke of a marketplace of ideas in which truth is tested by competition. Ronald Dworkin treated individual rights as trumps over collective goals.

questions.question: In Subramanian Swamy v Union (2016), the Court's treatment of criminal defamation shows that

options.A: reputation is part of the right under Article 21 and criminal defamation is a reasonable restriction within Article 19(2)
options.B: criminal defamation was held unconstitutional because a civil remedy is always sufficient
options.C: criminal defamation was upheld because Article 19(2) lists it alone, making any inquiry into reasonableness unnecessary
options.D: Article 19(1)(a) outweighs reputation in every case, so criminal defamation survives only for private persons and never for public ones

questions.explanation: The Court upheld criminal defamation as a reasonable restriction, resting reputation on Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D gives free speech absolute priority. Option C claims that Article 19(2) excludes reasonableness review. Option B reverses the outcome.
questions.clat_trap: 'every case', 'always' and 'never' mark overstatement.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which author's principle is most naturally invoked by a person who argues that the State may restrict speech only to prevent harm to others?

options.A: Austin's command theory, which makes the sovereign's command the only limit on speech
options.B: Justice Holmes's marketplace of ideas, which allows no restraint on any speech whatever
options.C: Lord Devlin's view that a society may enforce its shared public morality
options.D: John Stuart Mill's harm principle

questions.explanation: Mill's harm principle limits coercion to the prevention of harm to others.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C is a view about enforcing morality. Option B misstates Holmes by calling the marketplace absolute. Option A applies a positivist theory to a different question.
questions.clat_trap: All options name real jurists, so the stem must be read for the specific principle.
questions.language_trick: 'only to prevent harm' echoes the harm principle.

questions.question: A journalist publishes a true report on a minister's decision, in good faith and for the public good, which affects the minister's reputation. Under the defamation provisions described, the journalist

options.A: is liable unless the minister is shown to have suffered a financial loss measurable in money
options.B: is protected by the exception for a true imputation made for the public good, since truth alone is not a defence unless it also serves the public good
options.C: is protected only if the report was published after the minister's written permission to do so
options.D: is liable, because truth is never a defence to criminal defamation of a public servant, whose reputation is specially protected
